title: From proof of concept to production: the part that is not code
excerpt: My last post compared Director-Driven Development with other AI coding workflows and ended on a narrow claim: AI tools generate and review code, and my frameworks make the architecture and security requirements part of “done”. Writing it, I kept bumping into a bigger objection, my own: an app is so much more than the app. […]
content:
My last post compared Director-Driven Development with other AI coding workflows and ended on a narrow claim: AI tools generate and review code, and my frameworks make the architecture and security requirements part of “done”. Writing it, I kept bumping into a bigger objection, my own: an app is so much more than the app. In an enterprise, a proof of concept becomes production only when the infrastructure, the identities, the monitoring, the backups, the network, the people on call and the evidence for the auditor exist around it. CodeQL finds flaws in code. The door an attacker uses is often somewhere else.

So this post takes the wider view. What does production readiness mean beyond the code? What do the breach reports say about where things actually fail? What do AI coding tools cover at those layers, and what do enterprises use instead? And what does my SaaS framework, SaaSAllTheThings, actually do when you hand it your security framework, such as the ISF Standard of Good Practice? I read its latest release file by file to answer that last one, and the answer is narrower than what I had been saying. The research notes with every source are linked at the end.

What production means, beyond the code

There is no single checklist, so I used the ones enterprises already use to name the areas: the Azure Well-Architected pillars, the Cloud Adoption Framework’s landing-zone design areas, GDPR Articles 32 and 33, and the control titles of ISO/IEC 27002. The envelope around a business-critical system comes out as eight areas.

  • Infrastructure and change: environments as code, reviewed change, no drift between the template and the estate.
  • Monitoring and operations: observability, alert routes, incident response. GDPR gives a controller 72 hours from awareness to notify, so detection and escalation have to exist before go-live.
  • Compliance evidence: proof that controls operated over time, not only that they were designed.
  • Personal data: classification, minimisation, retention, residency, deletion.
  • Access: identities, MFA, least privilege, just-in-time access to production, periodic reviews. In every cloud service model the customer keeps the data, the configuration and the identities.
  • Continuity and recovery: recovery point and time, backups, and a restore that has been tested, which GDPR Article 32 asks for in as many words.
  • Networking: public access off, private endpoints, local authentication off, controlled egress.
  • Supply chain: dependencies, third parties, pipeline identity.

One judgment runs through all of them. A repository can hold the requirement, the design and the infrastructure code. It cannot hold the proof. Each of these areas is shown by a running system, its logs and a test performed on it.

Where things actually fail

The 2026 editions of the big incident reports agree on more than I expected, with two cautions: they measure different populations, so their numbers must not be added, and several figures below come from summaries because the full reports were not readable to me.

Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, covering more than 22,000 confirmed breaches, puts vulnerability exploitation first among entry points at 31 percent of breaches, ahead of stolen credentials for the first time in 19 years. A third party was involved in 48 percent of breaches. Mandiant’s M-Trends 2026, from more than 500,000 hours of incident response, also puts exploits first at 32 percent, for the sixth year running, with voice phishing second. Microsoft’s Digital Defense Report 2026 counts nearly 40,000 published vulnerabilities in the first half of the year, weaponised in well under 24 hours, while enterprise remediation of critical external vulnerabilities “can take 30 to 60 days”. IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach, from 602 breaches, puts the average cost at 4.99 million dollars and the time to identify and contain a breach at 247 days, the first rise in five years; 53 percent of the breached organisations lacked encryption for sensitive data at rest or in transit.

Read together, these say three things about people and process.

First, “exploitation” here is mostly not your application code. The named targets are edge devices, VPNs and deployed products, and the failure is a patch that took 30 to 60 days to land. That is exposure management, an operations discipline, and it fails for reasons of ownership and change control rather than coding skill. No report I read gives a share for flaws in the victim’s own application code, so I cannot put “code against everything else” in one number. What I can say is that code review alone addresses a minority of what these reports describe.

Second, identity and people are the other door: valid accounts, user execution, phishing by email and by phone, and a human element in a majority of breaches. Third-party involvement rose from 30 to 48 percent of breaches in one year. Those are process failures in onboarding, offboarding, access review and vendor management, and they happen in organisations with good code.

Third, detection is slow. 247 days to identify and contain, a median dwell of 14 days, 25 days before an outsider tells you. Monitoring and an incident process are not nice-to-haves after launch. They are the difference between an incident and a notification to the regulator.

On misconfiguration specifically, the only source that ranks it first is the Cloud Security Alliance’s survey of more than 500 experts, which is perception rather than incident data. I include it because its order matches what I see in practice: misconfiguration and weak change control, identity, insecure interfaces, and only in sixth place insecure software development.

What the tools cover at these layers

My earlier post found that the AI coding tools now ship real security features: Copilot’s cloud agent runs CodeQL, secret scanning and dependency checks by default; Devin reviews every pull request for security flaws and cannot be switched off; Cursor’s Bugbot and the newer Codex and Claude Code security scans look for vulnerabilities in source. Looked at against the envelope, they all sit in the same place: the editor and the pull request, on source code. CodeQL does not list Bicep, Terraform or ARM templates among its languages. Bugbot deliberately does not read credential-like files or Terraform state. Codex Security’s own documentation says a scan with no findings can still miss vulnerabilities, and none of them mentions infrastructure configuration, identity or runtime.

Enterprises close that gap with different tools at different stages. Azure Policy has built-in definitions such as “Cosmos DB should disable public network access” and “Key Vault should disable public network access”, and its Deny effect refuses the deployment before the resource provider ever sees it, while existing resources are only marked non-compliant. Microsoft Security DevOps scans infrastructure as code in the pipeline with Template Analyzer, Checkov and Terrascan. Defender for Cloud assesses the deployed estate continuously against standards such as ISO/IEC 27001 and NIST SP 800-53, and is honest that some controls cannot be assessed automatically. GitHub exports an SBOM from its dependency graph.

Neither set replaces the other. CodeQL cannot see a public endpoint, and Azure Policy cannot see an injection flaw. That is the first correction to my framing: a production-grade pipeline is a stack of gates at commit, at deploy and at run time, and no coding tool, mine included, covers more than one of them.

What SaaSAllTheThings does with your security framework

SaaSAllTheThings is my framework for B2B SaaS on Azure, built on the idea that the customer’s own security framework and control requirements live in the repository and shape every architecture decision. I had been describing that as a full supply-chain view that brings more security and easier compliance proof than other tools. Here is what the latest release actually does, from its files.

The path starts with a human. You name your security framework and the control frameworks that apply in the director brief, with the version, what applies and what evidence is expected from whom, and you put the requirement text or your own control list in a compliance folder. Nothing parses it. An assessment procedure reads the brief, scores nine dimensions, including configuration and secrets, identity, and delivery and operations, and picks workshops. The workshops cover vision and constraints, tenancy and identity with the security officer and the data protection officer in the room, integration and credentials, and operations: just-in-time production access, managed identities, Key Vault, a threat review of the target picture, recovery point and time, support and cost. Their outputs go into the requirements document, the decision log and draft architecture decision records.

Every architecture session then reads the compliance folder and the requirements document’s Data and Compliance section, flags a conflict between a requirement and the reference design, weighs each option against OWASP, least privilege, defence in depth, zero trust, data minimisation and “any standard named in the compliance requirements”, and states the security and compliance impact of each option. Only the human accepts the decision. The research procedure treats the customer’s security framework as the top-tier source, traces each requirement to a control, labels the trace as direct, partial, interpretive or unverified, and never lets text from the compliance folder into a public search.

Then there is the check. It fails the build on nine rules: layering, domain purity, two tenant-isolation rules, secrets patterns, file and host size, message versioning and cost-driven SKU choice. The only way past a failing rule is an accepted decision record naming the rule and the file, and a proposed decision does not count. That part holds, and I found nothing like it in the other tools.

Now the gaps, area by area against the envelope.

Two more limits belong here. The gate is a local pre-commit hook and, in Claude Code, a stop hook; no CI ships with the framework, so a passing check leaves no record off the developer’s machine unless the project adds one. And “only the human accepts a decision” rests on a rule and a hook that asks before writing “accepted”. The status is a line of text. Branch protection and pull request review are what make it binding, and the framework does not set those up for you.

The claims, checked

  • “A full supply-chain view.” Does not hold. For the delivery chain, requirement to commit, it holds in part: the records link a requirement to a decision to an item to a commit. For components and vendors, there is no SBOM, no dependency scanning, no provenance and no supplier assessment. I will stop saying it.
  • “More security than others.” Not as stated. The narrow version holds: tenant source, tenant branching, secret patterns and layering are enforced where other tools advise. The wide version fails: Copilot ships code scanning, secret scanning and dependency checks by default, and SaaSAllTheThings ships none of those. Proving “more” would take a measured comparison on sample applications and a penetration test.
  • “Easier compliance proof.” Plausible for design-stage evidence, unproven beyond it. The requirements and the named framework are in the repository, every architecture session reads them, and every deviation is a decision you accepted. No release maps a rule or a test to a control identifier, no auditor has read these records, and the operating evidence, access reviews, pipeline approvals, restore tests, comes from the running system.
  • “Cannot exfiltrate through public endpoints.” Not on the records. There is no network requirement and no rule for it.
  • “Production-ready.” No. Same answer as last time: that needs a deployment and an audit.

What does hold, in sentences I am comfortable publishing: your security and architecture requirements become design records and a build gate; the customer’s framework lives in the repository and every architecture session reads it; every decision and change leaves a record a reviewer can read; and the running system, not the repository, provides the operating evidence.

Does this change the equation?

Yes, in both directions. It makes the case for structure stronger: the breach reports say the failures that cost the most are failures of ownership, change control, access review and detection, and a workflow whose whole point is written requirements, named owners, accepted decisions and a gate is aimed at exactly that. It also makes my framework’s reach smaller than I was claiming. Of the eight areas, it enforces parts of three, advises on six, and is silent on networking and the component supply chain.

So the work is clear, and it is the same work for anyone taking an AI-built proof of concept toward production. On the framework side: a network posture topic with a rule on public network access and local authentication, a shipped CI workflow that keeps the check’s output as evidence, a seeded mapping table from control identifier to requirement to rule or test, a continuity topic with a restore-test item, and a dependency view. On the proof side: a pilot deployment with Azure Policy deny assignments and Defender for Cloud, tested from outside, and then an auditor reading the records. Until that pilot exists, the honest sentence is that the framework carries the requirements and the design to the commit, and the enterprise’s own platform controls and people carry them the rest of the way.

If you run a platform or a security function and would like to be that pilot, I would like to hear from you.

Sources

Breach and incident reports, read 21 October 2026: Verizon, 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report and its news release; IBM, Cost of a Data Breach 2026; Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2026; Mandiant M-Trends 2026; Cloud Security Alliance, Top Threats to Cloud Computing 2024. Several figures (human element, credential abuse, dwell time, IBM root causes) come from secondary summaries of these reports; the full reports were too large or unreadable in my tools.

Platform and standards: Azure Well-Architected pillars; Cloud Adoption Framework landing zone design areas; Shared responsibility in the cloud; Azure Policy deny effect and the Service Bus and Cosmos DB built-in definitions; Scan infrastructure as code with Microsoft Security DevOps; Service Bus private endpoints; Cosmos DB continuous backup; GDPR Articles 32 and 33; ISF Standard of Good Practice.

Tool documentation: CodeQL supported languages; GitHub secret scanning and SBOM export; Cursor Bugbot; Devin Review; Codex Security; Claude Code Security.

SaaSAllTheThings at its latest release: the repository, read file by file: rules, procedures, workshops, reference pages, templates, the check and its hooks. Nothing was run and no deployment was made; “not found” means not found in those files.

The research notes behind this post, with every claim, source, tier and confidence, and the open gaps: production readiness of AI coding tools and from proof of concept to production in an enterprise. title: Where Director-Driven Development sits among AI coding workflows
excerpt: What the AI coding tools and workflows of 2026 ship, what Director-Driven Development shares with them, where it stands alone, and which of my own claims survive the vendors’ documentation and the evidence on AI-generated code.
content:
I built Director-Driven Development because the second prompt kept going wrong: the fix after the demo, the feature on top of something that already worked. Since then the tools have moved fast, and I owed myself an honest look at what the alternatives do now, what my way of working shares with them, where it stands alone, and where it claims too much. This post is that look. It comes from reading the vendors’ own documentation and best-practice guides in October 2026, not from benchmarks, so it says what each one ships or prescribes, not how well it works.

The alternatives, in four groups: plain agent use (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot’s agent mode, Codex, Gemini CLI); spec-driven workflows (Kiro, GitHub’s spec-kit, the BMAD method, and published practitioner methods such as Addy Osmani’s and Harper Reed’s); agent harnesses (Aider, Cline, Roo Code, OpenHands); and autonomous agents (Devin, Codex cloud, Jules, Copilot’s cloud agent).

What is common practice now

Most of the ideas I started from are mainstream in 2026, and that is good news, not bad.

  • Verification as the core loop. Anthropic’s Claude Code guide opens with “give Claude a way to verify its work”; Devin’s guide asks for tests, linters and concrete pass conditions; Aider re-runs tests after every edit and tries to fix what fails. DDD’s check is the same idea with a fixed name and exit codes.
  • Spec first, small tasks, fresh contexts. Osmani, Reed, Kiro, spec-kit and the Claude guide (“interview you, write SPEC.md, start a fresh session”) all say it. DDD’s one-item-one-context is the same move.
  • Instruction files. AGENTS.md is read by Cursor, Codex and Jules, so my choice of it is no longer a choice.
  • Review in a fresh context. The Claude guide recommends an adversarial reviewer subagent in nearly the words of DDD’s review rule.
  • Hooks for guarantees. The same guide draws the line I draw: instruction files are advisory, hooks are deterministic.

If you are doing those five things with any tool, you are most of the way to this way of working already.

Where it stands alone, as far as I could find

Reading overview pages, not every sub-page, these were not found anywhere else:

  • A decision log tied to dated research notes, each with its sources, confidence and a “verified as of” date, so a later session reuses the evidence instead of redoing it.
  • A size-keyed model map with a one-step escalation and a two-attempt stop. Cline and Roo pick a model per mode, Osmani per task; none ties it to a written size scale with a retry rule.
  • A named drift reset that only the director can start, beside a routine alignment pass over the records and the code. Kiro and spec-kit check a spec’s internal consistency, which is narrower.
  • An ownership table with placeholders for what the human owns, backed by a hook that blocks the agent from the director’s own workspace.
  • Architecture rules inside the build check, with an accepted decision record as the only way past them. The Claude guide tells you to write such hooks yourself; spec-kit’s gates are checkboxes in a template that the model fills in.

The honest qualifier: “not found” on the pages I read, and vendors ship monthly.

Where others do more

  • Isolation and scale: OS-level sandboxes, cloud runs, parallel worktrees, agent teams and batch fan-out in Claude Code; Copilot’s ephemeral cloud environment; Jules’s virtual machine. DDD runs where you run it.
  • Autonomous loops with an evaluator and a permissions classifier.
  • Spec depth: Kiro’s wave-based parallel tasks and property-based tests, spec-kit’s presets and extensions, BMAD’s multi-role sessions.
  • Team enforcement: Cursor’s enforced team rules, Copilot’s organisation instructions and rulesets.
  • Rewind: checkpoints that restore both the conversation and the code.
  • Tool reach: IDE integration, MCP servers, plugin marketplaces. DDD ships as Markdown, shell and skills, with no IDE surface, and its enforcement exists only in the three domains it has frameworks for: Godot games, small apps, B2B SaaS on Azure.

The claim I wanted to make, and what survives

My working line was: others help you make something that works; DDD gets you to software you can prove is stable, tested and compliant. Checked against what the vendors ship, half of that is wrong.

“Others stop at working” is false. GitHub’s Copilot cloud agent runs CodeQL, secret scanning and dependency checks by default, needs a human to approve its workflow runs, and cannot approve or merge its own pull request. Devin’s review scans every pull request for security issues and cannot be turned off. Claude Code’s hooks can fail a turn until a check passes. Every vendor also puts the final review of the output with you, in writing.

What they don’t ship is the package: architecture rules as part of “done”, exceptions only through a decision record you accept, and the customer’s own security framework living in the repository where every architecture session reads it. That is what SaaSAllTheThings does, and I did not find it elsewhere.

“Provably stable” and “compliant” don’t survive either. I have no production deployment data, no independent quality measurement and no audit. The vendors’ SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certificates cover their services, not the software built with them, and no regulation I read requires a particular gate on AI-written code; a customer’s control framework and its auditor decide what evidence counts. My own earlier post said that people own compliance, not the framework. It still does.

The evidence that a gate matters, though, is real and independent of me. Veracode found security flaws in 45 percent of its tests of AI-generated code, with newer and larger models no better. CodeRabbit counted 1.7 times the issues per AI co-authored pull request, and 1.6 times the security issues, in 470 pull requests with authorship inferred. DORA associates a 25 percent rise in AI adoption with 7 percent less delivery stability. A study of 4,022 agent pull requests found a security smell in 39 percent, and that human review missed 81 percent of the hard-coded credentials among them. Review alone does not catch this; a deterministic check does, which is the whole argument for putting the rules in the check.

So the line that holds is shorter: AI tools generate and review; Director-Driven Development makes the architecture and security requirements part of done, and leaves records a reviewer can read. Anything stronger needs a production run or an audit, and I will write that post when I have one.

Sources

Vendor documentation, read 19 and 20 October 2026: Anthropic, Best practices for Claude Code and Claude Code security; GitHub, about the Copilot cloud agent and its risks and mitigations page; GitHub spec-kit and its spec-driven.md; Kiro specs and hooks; BMAD method; Cursor rules and Bugbot; OpenAI Codex, AGENTS.md and security; Jules; Devin, instructing Devin and Devin Review; Cline, plan and act; Roo Code modes; Aider, lint and test; Gemini CLI context files; OpenHands.

Practitioner methods: Addy Osmani, my AI coding workflow; Harper Reed, my LLM codegen workflow.

Evidence on AI-generated code: Veracode, GenAI Code Security Report 2025; CodeRabbit, State of AI vs human code; GitClear, AI code quality 2025; DORA, the impact of generative AI in software development; security smells in agent pull requests, arXiv 2607.12428; Perry et al., do users write more insecure code with AI assistants, arXiv 2211.03622. Regulation and standards consulted: NIST SP 800-218A, EU AI Act, Article 15.

The two research notes behind this post, with the full comparison matrix and the gaps in what was read, are in the Director-Driven Development repository: the comparison and production readiness.

title: What directing AI agents costs: three projects, measured
excerpt: Three projects run on Director-Driven Development, every token priced at API rates: $2 to $3 per completed task, $50 for a 6,700-line feature, 96 percent cache reads, and what a Claude Max subscription turns that into.
content:
Everyone building with AI coding agents has an opinion about what it costs. I had one too. So I measured it instead: three projects, every token, priced at the public API rates, over the 24 days since the first commit of the largest one. This post is the result, with the conclusions I think the numbers support and the ones they don’t.

The three projects all run on Director-Driven Development: I direct, agents build, one automatic check decides when a task is done, and every decision is written down. If you haven’t read about it, the original post explains the why and the docs explain the how.

  • Director-Driven Development itself: the documentation site, which also builds and releases the three frameworks (Godot-Director, App-Director, SaaSAllTheThings) from its own task queue. Nine days.
  • PKSEI, a comedy rage game in which four friends paddle a canoe catamaran across a lake, built in two and a half days and playable on itch.io. Its devlog tells the story; the repository holds the records.
  • Lantern, a codename: a larger indie game, 24 days in and not yet announced. Its code base is about half done in technical functionality; the assets, the playtesting and the tuning come later.

How I measured

Claude Code keeps a transcript of every session on disk, including the subagents a session starts, and every reply in it carries the token counts: fresh input, output, cache writes, cache reads, and the model that produced it. I summed them, one entry per message, and priced them at the pay-as-you-go API rates on claude.com/pricing as of 19 October 2026: Fable 5.1 at $10 in and $50 out per million tokens, Opus 5.5 at $4 and $20, Sonnet 5.5 at $2 and $10, Haiku 5.5 at $0.10 and $0.50, with cache reads at a tenth to a fortieth of the input price and cache writes at 1.25 times it. The script is in the repository: tools/usage.py.

One thing to hold on to for the rest of the post: none of this was billed per token. All three projects ran on a Claude Max subscription. The dollar figures are what the same tokens would have cost on the API: a measure of the size of the work, not of money spent. The money comes at the end.

The numbers

What those tasks produced: a 44,000-word documentation site; 20 framework releases, including Godot-Director’s auto-playtesting (14,000 new lines); a 22,000-line game with its tests, generated art and sound, shipped to itch.io about twenty times.

“Hours at the keyboard” is every wait of thirty minutes or less that ended with a message from me: reading the agent’s report, deciding, typing. “On its own” is the rest of the time between events, the agent generating, running tools and waiting for its builders. Neither counts what happens away from the keyboard: playing the game on a phone, thinking, reviewing pull requests on GitHub. So my real hours are higher, by one to two on PKSEI alone by my own estimate, and the per-hour figures are upper bounds. The PKSEI devlog counts permission approvals as keyboard time too and gets 4.7 hours; the transcripts can’t tell an approval from a tool finishing, so this post leaves them out.

One source note: the PKSEI devlog quotes Claude Code’s own session report, $258 and 1.67 million output tokens for the build. The transcripts, which this post uses for all three projects so they compare, give $244 and 1.73 million; the two agree within six percent, the difference being two commits made after the report.

Where the money goes

Cache reads are 96 to 97 percent of the tokens and between a third and a half of the cost. Fresh input is nothing: my messages are a sentence or two. Output, which is all the code, tests, records and reports plus the models’ thinking, is half a percent of the tokens and 13 to 27 percent of the cost. The rest is cache writes: every builder that starts in a fresh context writes the records it reads into the cache, 80,000 tokens for a small item, a million for a large one.

The surprise was who spends it. The orchestrating session, the one I talk to, accounts for 60 to 72 percent of the cost in all three projects. The builders, reviewers and researchers it starts are the rest. The orchestrator designs, keeps the records, reads every report, writes every commit and pull request.

What a change costs

A task is small by design, so a cost per task is partly a statement about how I cut the work. Merged changes are the unit other people publish, so here are seven of mine from the three projects, large to small, measured from the moment the first builder started to the moment the change was committed or its pull request opened. The design conversation before the builder isn’t in these numbers; the builders, the reviewers and the orchestrator’s bookkeeping are. The sources at the end name each one.

A third of a cent to two cents per line added, around a cent for anything over a hundred lines, and the orchestrator’s share grows as the change shrinks. One change is left out of the table and the charts because it is an order of magnitude larger than a typical task: a 6,687-line framework feature built in five commits, two of them with an independent Opus review, which cost $50 of API-equivalent and twenty minutes of my attention spread over four hours, at the same rate per line as the rest.

The published comparison is Jellyfish’s, from 12,000 developers in the first quarter of 2026, at list prices: cost per merged pull request from $0.28 in their cheapest tier to $89 in their most expensive, with a median of about 7 million tokens per pull request and 69 million in the top decile. They don’t say how big their pull requests are. Mine run from $0.29 to $7.90 with the size stated, and the one large feature, at $50, used twice the tokens of their top decile. One practitioner ran the same real feature 29 times through a dozen agents and harnesses and got $3 to $33 per merged feature. One developer published his own two months on Claude Code with a spec-driven workflow, which is close to mine: $36 per commit, $314 per day, with commits six to thirteen times the size of mine in output tokens. Per token of output we’re of the same order; per commit I’m far cheaper because my commits are far smaller.

The same data on a linear scale, which is how the difference looks when the axis is money rather than ratios:

What the way of working does to the bill

Three things in the workflow show up in the numbers, and one thing I expected doesn’t.

It is cache-friendly. Without caching, the same tokens would cost eleven to twelve times more: $4,532, $2,847 and $11,773. Caching is Anthropic’s feature and any Claude Code session gets it, so I won’t claim the saving as mine. What the workflow contributes is stable context: the rules, the records and the task list live in files that every session and every builder reads the same way, so almost everything a model sees, it has seen before.

Small tasks, one commit each, keep the per-task cost flat. $2.08, $2.56 and $2.65 for three projects of very different size and shape. That consistency is the most useful number in this post, and it is partly a property of how the work is cut: a task is sized to fit one builder in one fresh context, and the size picks the model.

The director’s hours are the limit, not the tokens. At $20 to $85 of API-equivalent per hour at the keyboard, with the agent working one and a half to five hours on its own for each of mine, a full day of directing is a $200 to $700 day, and I can’t direct more than a day a day. The one week I ran three sessions in parallel is the week the bill was highest.

Model sizing saves less than I thought. Sending small items to Haiku and medium ones to Sonnet saved about 9 percent against running everything on Opus. The builders aren’t where the tokens are; the orchestrator is, and its model is the biggest single cost choice. In PKSEI I ran the orchestrator on Fable 5.1 on purpose, because I had weekly allowance to spare and wanted to try it: $136 of the project’s $244. The same session on Opus would have been about $55. I also found a mistake there: 48 of the 89 builder runs had inherited Fable from the session instead of getting the model their size called for, $94, nearly forty percent of the project’s cost, for no reason. The fix is a rule now queued in all three frameworks: a builder always gets its model passed explicitly. And a confession about the orchestrator: since moving to Max I have run design sessions on Opus and Fable because the allowance was there, not because the work needed it. Everything on Sonnet 5.5, orchestrator included, would have cost $198, $80 and $581 instead of $364, $244 and $1,067: a third to a half. I haven’t measured what that does to quality, so it’s a floor, not a recommendation.

What the subscription turns it into

Here is the money. Anthropic publishes the plan prices and the session multiples (Max 5x and Max 20x are five and twenty times Pro per five-hour window), not the weekly caps. Third-party measurements from real accounts fill the gap; the week of 12 October 2026, Wokey measured Pro’s weekly cap at about $170 of API-equivalent across 474 accounts and Max 20x at about $1,640 across 17. My own heaviest week, $1,155 across six projects with allowance left, agrees with the 20x figure.

If the weekly limit is used, every plan delivers its tokens at roughly a thirtieth of the API price. The $2 to $3 per completed task becomes six to eight cents. The $50 feature pull request becomes a dollar and a half. The $20 to $85 per hour at the keyboard becomes under a dollar to two and a half.

Which plan fits: at $20 to $85 an hour at the keyboard, a Pro week covers two to eight hours of directing, a Max 5x week roughly six to forty, a Max 20x week twenty to seventy-five. The five-hour window binds first on Pro: about $14 of API value, which this way of working spends in well under an hour. So Pro suits a few hours a week in short sittings, Max 5x a part-time director, and Max 20x a full-time one, parallel sessions, and Fable, which on Max may use half the weekly cap at no extra charge but moves the meter about twice as fast as Opus. Past any cap, extra usage is billed at API rates.

How it sits next to what others measure

The structural numbers agree with outside data: Cursor reports that about 90 percent of its tokens are cache reads across two years of aggregate use, Jellyfish reports 96 percent across its customers, and an academic study of agent runs on SWE-bench finds cache reads the largest token category in every phase; my 96 to 97 percent fits. The cost-per-change comparison is the one above, and it is the one the claim rests on.

The productivity numbers don’t line up, because there’s nothing to line them up with. The large studies measure time on task, tasks or pull requests per developer, and cycle time, and they disagree: controlled trials range from 19 percent slower (METR’s 2025 trial of experienced developers in their own repositories) to 56 percent faster (a one-task trial with hired programmers); the telemetry studies that also count review load and defects find those rising faster than output. None joins billed cost to merged changes on real projects, no one reports work per million tokens, and no study separates a structured workflow from freeform use on cost or output, which is the measurement this post would need to claim more than it does. So I won’t put my 142 tasks in nine days next to anyone’s uplift figure. The honest comparison is the one above: same token shape, and pull requests inside the only published cost range, with their sizes stated and most of theirs not.

The conclusions

Director-Driven Development is an efficient way to turn attention into shipped work. Not because of a trick with models, but because the whole loop is built to be cached, cut small and recorded: a completed task costs $2 to $3 of API-equivalent whether it’s a docs page, a game rule with its tests, or a framework release; a 6,700-line feature with its tests costs $50 and twenty minutes of attention; and the records show where every dollar went. The bill scales with my hours, which is the constraint I’d choose.

Claude Code on a subscription is remarkable value for this way of working. Used to its weekly cap, a plan delivers tokens at about three cents on the API dollar; a few hours a week fit in Pro, a part-time director in Max 5x, and a full-time one, parallel sessions or Fable call for 20x.

And what I’m not claiming, because I didn’t measure it: that this is cheaper than building the same things another way, by hand or with an agent and no workflow. There is no baseline in these numbers, and no one has published one. Nor do they say anything about quality: PKSEI still has 116 placeholder values, and the frameworks’ /ui-design feature is still in my own acceptance test. The numbers say what three real projects cost, to the token, and that the cost was flat, predictable and small next to the subscription that paid for it.

Measure your own

The transcripts are in ~/.claude/projects/. The script that produced every number here, tools/usage.py in the Director-Driven Development repository, prints the same table for any project on your machine: the total at dated prices, the shares by token kind and by session, your hours at the keyboard, and what it would have cost uncached or on one model. Date your prices, state whether you mean API-equivalent or money, and keep the orchestrator’s model in view: it’s where the tokens are.

Sources

The seven changes: samples 1, 2, 3 and 7 are PKSEI commits 54daa59, a63c993, b637d7a and e66b0aa; 4 is App-Director #22 with SaaSAllTheThings #15; 5 and 6 are Godot-Director #27 and #29. The large feature left out of the charts is Godot-Director #25.

The published figures: Jellyfish, “Is tokenmaxxing cost effective?” (April 2026) and its State of AI in Software Engineering report for the cache-read share; Insight, “Token Price Is the Wrong Number” (July 2026); Zest’s Claude Code pricing page; arXiv 2607.13080 (one developer, two 28-day periods, spec-driven); Cursor’s usage data via The Pragmatic Engineer; arXiv 2604.22750 on token use in agent runs; METR’s 2025 trial and the 2023 Copilot trial for the range of productivity findings; Wokey’s measured usage limits for the weekly caps; claude.com/pricing for the API prices and plans; the PKSEI devlog for the game’s own report. All read on 19 October 2026.

title: Anchoring AI-built SaaS in your security framework
excerpt: When an AI agent writes most of your code, your security framework has to live where the agent works. How SaaSAllTheThings anchors a B2B SaaS in your control framework: enforce what’s critical, audit the rest.
content:
When an AI agent writes most of your code, your security framework can’t sit in a document the agent never sees. It has to live where the agent works: in the repo, in the decisions it brings to you, and in the checks it can’t get past.

I’ve spent the last five years building cloud platforms for banks, insurance and government. The principle that runs through all of it is simple: trust, but verify. We anchor the platform in a control framework, enforce the controls that matter most, and audit the rest. Nobody has to remember every control. The platform does.

AI coding agents need the same thing, and more urgently. An agent works fast, never gets tired and never reads the wiki. Every change it makes looks reasonable on its own, and that is exactly how a platform slowly drifts away from its security framework.

This post shows how SaaSAllTheThings, my open-source framework for building B2B SaaS on Azure with Director-Driven Development, anchors a product in your security framework, in two layers:

  • Enforce what’s critical. A small set of rules is checked by machine, on every change, and an agent cannot get past them.
  • Audit the rest. Everything that needs judgement is put in front of you, the director, with the requirements quoted, before the decision is made.

If you’re new to the framework, the step-by-step guide covers the basics.

1. Give requirements a home

An agent can only respect a requirement it can find. In SaaSAllTheThings, compliance requirements live in plain files in the app’s own repo, next to the code:

  • product/prd.md › Data and Compliance: data residency, retention, which data is personal, audit needs, and export and deletion when a customer leaves.
  • compliance/: the control framework you’re held to, such as the ISF Standard of Good Practice or ISO 27001, and the security requirements in your customer contracts. This is the anchor every architecture decision is checked against.
  • product/requirements/: user stories and feature specs, when you have them.

The framework asks for these early. Onboarding includes data and compliance in its product interview, and the tenancy and identity workshop ends with a data map: each kind of data, who owns it, whether it’s personal and how long it’s kept.

Anything you haven’t decided stays visibly undecided. The reference is explicit: until the PRD decides retention, residency and which fields are personal, they’re open questions, not guesses. An agent never picks a retention period because it seemed reasonable.

2. Enforce what’s critical

A handful of security controls are too important to depend on anyone remembering them, human or agent. SaaSAllTheThings builds them into the architecture and enforces them by machine, in two places. These are built into the check and the hooks: the small set of controls every SaaS on this architecture needs, whatever framework you answer to.

The check runs before every commit that touches code, and in Claude Code also before the agent ends its turn. Among its architecture rules, these carry the security weight:

The hooks stop commands before they run. An agent can’t read a Key Vault secret into its session, create a client secret (it has to use a federated credential), delete Azure resources, run a complete-mode deployment, force-push, or skip the check with --no-verify. Two more actions don’t block but ask you first: editing the framework’s own files, and marking an ADR as accepted.

None of this depends on the agent following instructions. A prompt can be ignored; a failing build can’t.

3. Audit the rest

Most compliance questions can’t be reduced to a pattern a script can match. Should this data be stored in another region? Is this integration allowed to see personal data? Those need judgement, and in Director-Driven Development judgement belongs to the director. The framework’s job is to make sure you never decide blind.

When an architecture question comes up, /architect prepares the call before it offers anything:

  1. It reads your requirements. The reference topic in question, every related ADR, compliance/, product/requirements/ and the PRD’s Data and Compliance section.
  2. It classifies the question: an open choice, a deviation from the reference, a gap in the framework, or a requirements conflict, where the compliant architecture would break a stated requirement, or a requirement forces a deviation.
  3. It shows you the context first. The rule in question, the classification, related ADRs, and any conflict stated explicitly, before a single option is on the table.
  4. It offers 2-4 options, each with its effort, monthly Azure cost, risk, security and compliance impact, and how hard it is to undo.
  5. It checks every option against a standing baseline: OWASP Top 10, least privilege, defence in depth, zero trust, data minimisation, and the control framework in compliance/, whether that’s the ISF Standard of Good Practice, ISO 27001, SOC 2 or GDPR.
  6. It recommends one, preferring the option that complies, the one that can be undone, and the stronger security posture when the effort is similar. Then it waits for you.

The same discipline continues into the build. Large items, and any medium item that touches tenant isolation, identity, a contract or a stored schema, get an independent, read-only reviewer in a fresh context before they are committed.

4. Build personal data in from the start

GDPR-style requirements are hard to retrofit, so the reference architecture bakes the basics in from the first commit:

  • No personal data in logs, traces or metrics. Log ids, not names, email addresses or document contents. No secrets or tokens either.
  • No personal data in partition keys, where it would be copied into indexes and hard to erase.
  • Events carry personal data only where a consumer needs it. Messages travel further than you think.
  • Deletion is a platform capability. Deleting a tenant’s or a person’s data is built as part of the platform, not a script someone runs by hand.
  • Export and deletion are a milestone. The roadmap’s second-tenant stage isn’t done until a second customer sees none of the first one’s data, and export and deletion work.
  • Isolation is tested before a customer arrives. /tenant won’t call a new customer ready unless every store has a tenant-isolation test. A missing one is a high-severity bug.

And when a customer needs more than pooled tenancy allows, such as dedicated infrastructure for a regulated tenant, the architecture is ready for it: a tenant can move to its own deployment. Whether that’s worth the cost is a product decision, made by you, with the price on the table.

5. Make every deviation leave a trail

In a regulated environment, the question is rarely “did you follow the rule?” It’s “when you didn’t, who decided, why, and what did it cost?” SaaSAllTheThings answers that from the repo itself:

/align keeps the trail honest between audits. It reports stale ADR exceptions, proposed ADRs that have waited more than a week, and decisions the PRD no longer reflects.

The point isn’t paperwork. Every record is something the agent needs anyway to work in a fresh context, so the audit trail costs nothing extra to keep.

6. Treat drift in tenancy as a security finding

Agents don’t break your design in one go. They drift: a principle that can be read two ways eventually gets read two ways. For product rules, that’s a design problem. For tenancy and identity, it’s a security problem, and the framework treats it as one.

When you start a design drift reset with /drift-reset, the analysis of the system as built always includes tenancy and identity as an area of its own: where the tenant comes from at every entry point, whether every store, query, blob path, cache key and message carries it, how tokens are validated, and anything that reads across tenants. Drift found there is marked as a security finding and reported to you at once.

It doesn’t become a design question, because the reference has already settled it. It goes straight into the queue as a high-severity bug, ahead of everything else in the rebuild. Accepted ADRs are checked the same way: each one must still be honoured, and a reset can never drop one without a new ADR.

Three things a reset is never allowed to do: propose a change to the tenancy, identity or cost rules, relax a rule in the check, or add an exception. The postmortem goes the other way. It repeats the tenancy and identity analysis on everything the rebuild touched, and turns drift a script could have caught into proposed new check rules for you to approve. Repeated judgement becomes a check.

What stays human

A framework doesn’t make a product compliant. People do. What SaaSAllTheThings does is make sure the human decisions are the ones that count, and that they can be found again:

  • You decide the data rules: residency, retention, what’s personal, what an auditor needs to see.
  • You accept every deviation, with its cost and risk in front of you.
  • You approve every commit, and production deployments are yours to run.
  • You onboard customers. Consent, role assignments and the registry entry are steps the framework writes out for you, not steps it takes.

Everything else is either enforced by the build or put in front of you before it matters. Enforce what’s critical, audit the rest.

It’s the same principle we’ve used on regulated cloud platforms for years. The difference is that an agent only knows what’s in front of it, so your requirements have to live in the repo, and your critical controls in the build.

SaaSAllTheThings is free and MIT licensed: github.com/Freakling/SaaSAllTheThings. If you’re building SaaS for a regulated industry and want to compare notes, I’m happy to talk.

Trust the agent. Verify with the build.

  • Reviews: section 3
  • Deviation is an ADR and Records in files: section 5
  • /align and /drift-reset: sections 5 and 6

title: Build a B2B SaaS on Azure with Director-Driven Development
excerpt: A step-by-step guide to SaaSAllTheThings: build a multi-tenant B2B SaaS on Azure with an AI coding agent, where you own the product, the framework owns the architecture, and the build verifies every change.
content:
SaaSAllTheThings turns an idea, a proof of concept or an existing app into a multi-tenant B2B SaaS on Azure, with an AI coding agent doing the building and you directing it. It is free, MIT licensed and runs locally in your app’s own git repository.

In my Director-Driven Development post I described a way of working where you stop writing the implementation and become the director. SaaSAllTheThings is that way of working applied to the hardest kind of product I know: software that many business customers share, sign in to with their own identity provider, and trust with their data.

The framework splits the work three ways:

The middle column is the unusual part. The architecture isn’t up for debate in every session, because the check enforces it, so your attention goes to the product.

This guide walks through it step by step, from an empty repo to a running, released stage. The commands are Claude Code slash commands; every one of them also works as a plain sentence (“do the next task”), and the core works with any assistant that reads AGENTS.md.

Step 1: Pick your starting point and install

There are two ways in, and they meet at the same place.

  • From scratch. A short product interview, then the platform is built in small, proven steps, starting with tenancy and sign-in rather than bolting them on later.
  • From a proof of concept or an existing app. Assess it first. The saas-assessment skill reads the app without changing it and writes a report: how ready it is (scored, with evidence), a roadmap by stage with rough effort, the decisions to make, and the workshops to hold. Ask it “what does it take to make this app a SaaS?”

Your app needs git with no uncommitted changes, bash (Git for Windows includes it) and your backend’s toolchain, the .NET SDK 8+ for the default stack. Then, in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add Freakling/SaaSAllTheThings
/plugin install saasallthethings@saasallthethings

Open a new session in your app’s folder and run /saasallthethings:saas-all-the-things. Onboarding works out whether this is a new app, an existing one or an upgrade, and then:

  1. installs the files into your repo;
  2. settles the backend stack with you, keeping yours if it’s compatible;
  3. interviews you about the product, or reads the existing app, including its single-tenant habits and secrets;
  4. writes the first stages of the roadmap into TASKS.md;
  5. ends with one commit for you to approve.

Restart Claude Code so the new commands load. Using another assistant? Onboarding installs the tool-neutral core only, and your assistant follows AGENTS.md.

Step 2: Describe the product, one decision at a time

The product is yours, so the agent never decides a business rule on its own. Start a design session on any capability:

/design orders

Every product question comes back to you as 2-4 options with a recommendation, and you can always write your own answer. The agent proposes. The director decides. Your choices land in three plain files:

  • product/prd.md: the product’s current requirements, plus its open questions;
  • product/decisions.md: why, one line per decision;
  • TASKS.md: the items the decision creates.

Anything not decided yet goes on the open-questions list as Q<n>, and values you haven’t set are marked PLACEHOLDER in the code. /design questions ranks the open questions by what they unblock, so you know which decision to make next.

You don’t need a terminal for this part. The saas-design-session skill runs the same sessions in the Claude apps, on desktop, web or mobile, and it also prepares and scribes workshops with customers: agenda, pre-reads, timekeeping and decisions. Drop the notes into assessment/workshops/ and “process the workshop notes” turns them into records.

When a design session’s commit lands, clear the conversation. Every decision is in the files, so the next session loses nothing.

Step 3: Let the framework own the architecture

You don’t design the architecture from scratch each time. SaaSAllTheThings ships a reference architecture in .satt/reference/, one topic per file, and the agent reads only the topics an item touches:

  • Layers: contracts, domain, application, infrastructure, integration, host, platform and client, each allowed to depend only on the layers the reference lists. The domain is pure; the Azure Functions hosts stay thin.
  • Event-driven: commands on queues, events on topics (Service Bus), state and its events saved together through an outbox, idempotent consumers, versioned contracts.
  • Clients: a Windows app and a mobile app, separate and thin, depending on the contracts only.
  • Cost: Flex Consumption Functions, serverless Cosmos DB, one Service Bus namespace, log caps and a budget per environment.

When a build can’t comply, it stops and asks. You change the architecture for one app through an architecture session:

/architect

It writes an architecture decision record in adr/. Option one is always “comply with the reference”, so a deviation has to earn its place, with its cost in effort and monthly Azure spend. An ADR stays proposed until you accept it; in Claude Code a hook asks you before any ADR is marked accepted. If the deviation would fail the check, the ADR names it in a line like this:

- Exception: <rule> <path pattern>

The check excuses a violation only while an accepted ADR names it. Deviation becomes a decision, not an accident.

Step 4: Get tenancy, identity and integrations right first

The parts that make SaaS hard are the parts most often bolted on last. SaaSAllTheThings builds them first and checks them by machine.

  • Tenancy is pooled. The tenant comes from the validated token, never from the request. Every record and message carries it. Tenants differ by data in a registry, never by code, and a tenant can move to its own deployment later.
  • Identity is OIDC with Entra ID, multi-tenant, so customers sign in with their own directory (External ID for those without one). Clients use auth code with PKCE. Managed identities and federated credentials everywhere: no secrets in code, config or apps.
  • Integrations get a contract you decide: direction, system of record and conflict handling, then one anti-corruption layer and function app per external system. /integrate navision starts with Navision (Dynamics NAV / Business Central).
  • Data rules are product decisions. Residency, retention, which fields are personal, audit needs, and export and deletion when a customer leaves all live in the PRD’s Data and Compliance section, and stay open questions until you decide them. Personal data

This is what the check does when someone, human or agent, reads the tenant from a request header. Real output from the framework’s example app:

check: architecture violations (only an accepted ADR in adr/ excuses one; see .satt/procedures/architect.md):
  [tenant-source] src/OrderDesk.Functions/Orders/PlaceOrderFunction.cs:30: the tenant comes from the validated token, never from the request
check: architecture: FAIL: 1 violations

A second rule, tenant-branching, fails tenant-specific ifs in the code. In Claude Code, a hook also blocks reading Key Vault secrets and creating client secrets.

When your first customer is ready, /tenant runs a readiness check (isolation tests on every store, no tenant-specific code, a decided plan, identity, integrations) and writes out the steps only you can take: the registry entry, the consent link for the customer’s admin, role assignments and a smoke test. Onboarding a tenant changes no code.

Step 5: Plan one stage at a time

Every SaaSAllTheThings project goes through the same stages, so any session knows where the project stands. Existing apps start with stage 0, new ones at stage 1, and stages 4-6 can run side by side once the first slice works.

/roadmap writes items for the current stage and the next one only. Later stages wait, so they can be planned with what the earlier ones teach. Each item is small, sized and explicit about its scope:

### T12 · Place an order through the API · todo · M · agent
- Depends on: T10
- Touches: src/OrderDesk.Application/Orders/PlaceOrderHandler.cs (new), …
- Done when: an order without lines is rejected (test) · OrderPlacedV1 is saved with the order (test) · POST /api/v1/orders answers 201 in dev (demo)
- PRD: Capabilities › Orders

Touches names every file the item may change. Done when lists one to three observable outcomes, each tagged with how it’s proven. Large items are split before they start: contract first, then domain and application, then the host, then the client. Things only you can do, like app registrations or customer conversations, become human items in the same queue.

Step 6: Direct the build loop

Now the agent builds. One command picks the next ready item, high-severity bugs first:

/next-task

Or say “work through the queue”, and it keeps going until an item needs you. Each item runs the same loop:

  1. Hand off. The main session claims the item and hands it to a builder subagent that starts with an empty context. The builder reads only what the item needs: the files in Touches, the relevant architecture rows, the PRD sections it names and the reference topics it touches.
  2. Build on the right model. Each size maps to its own model: Haiku for XS and S, Sonnet for M, Opus for L and XL. A failed build retries once on the next size up.
  3. Prove. The builder runs bash tools/check.sh: the architecture rules, then the stack’s build and tests, then the Bicep files, then any app-specific checks. “It compiled” is not an answer.
  4. Review what’s risky. L and XL items, and M items that touch a contract, tenant isolation, identity or a stored schema, get an independent reviewer subagent in its own fresh context before the commit. Findings in scope are rebuilt; anything outside the item becomes a new item.
  5. Commit. You approve it. One item, one commit.

The main session never reads the code being changed. After each item it keeps only the builder’s report of about 20 lines, so a session that works through ten items stays about as lean as one that did one. When a session ends, nothing is lost: TASKS.md, the commits, the PRD and the ADRs hold everything.

The check also runs in a git pre-commit hook, and in Claude Code before the agent ends its turn. A force push, reset --hard, --no-verify and deleting Azure resources are blocked outright.

Step 7: Prove it with people, then release

A passing check proves the code does what the item said. It doesn’t prove the product works for a customer. Two more loops close that gap:

  • Acceptance (/acceptance): a checklist of what’s been built that needs a human eye in a running app. You tick Works or Broken, and broken rules come back as bugs.
  • Feedback (/feedback): turns a customer or pilot session into bugs, score trends and product proposals. Proposals come to you as design calls, like everything else in the product.

Releasing is a guided procedure, not a script you run blind:

/release dev

It runs the check, a what-if of the infrastructure changes, the deploy and a smoke test, and asks for your approval at each step. Deploys and cloud changes always ask you first, and production is yours to run.

Step 8: Align often, reset when you have to

Agents don’t break your design. They drift. A principle that can be read two ways eventually gets read two ways.

Align often. /align is a routine consistency pass across the PRD, decisions, ADRs, integration contracts, TASKS.md and the code. Every capability rule is built, planned or reported as a gap, every recent decision is reflected in the PRD, every project in the solution has a row in the architecture table, the architecture check passes and no proposed ADR has waited more than a week. Mechanical drift gets fixed; anything that touches the product or the architecture comes back to you. When the same conflict keeps returning, align recommends a reset.

Reset when you have to. /drift-reset is for when everything is accounted for, but a principle has been built two different ways. Only you can start it:

  1. Describe the system as built, area by area, with tenancy and identity always as an area of its own.
  2. Map how each pillar, PRD rule, contract rule and ADR was actually interpreted, and classify it as consistent, divergent or contradictory.
  3. Rewrite the design where it splits, one design call at a time.
  4. Plan the rebuild as ordinary items. No code is written in the reset itself.
  5. Run /drift-reset postmortem after the rebuild. Drift a script could have caught becomes a proposed check rule.

In SaaSAllTheThings a reset only covers the product you own. It never relaxes a check rule or touches the tenancy, identity and cost rules. Tenancy drift found in step 1 isn’t a design question at all: it’s a security finding, and it goes straight into the queue as a high-severity bug.

Try it

The fastest way to see what a project looks like is the worked example in the repository, examples/order-desk: a small order app with its PRD, decisions, ADRs, tasks and check settings in place. To watch the check work, clone the repository and run bash selftest.sh. It installs the framework into copies of the example and runs the architecture check, the hooks and the installer, with no Azure account needed.

Then pick your door:

  • A new product: install the plugin, run /saasallthethings:saas-all-the-things, and answer the product interview.
  • An existing app: run the saas-assessment skill first and read the report before you install anything.
  • Not ready for code yet: use saas-design-session in the Claude app to work through the product and architecture decisions, or to prepare a workshop with your team.

SaaSAllTheThings is free and MIT licensed: github.com/Freakling/SaaSAllTheThings. If you try it on a real product, I’d like to hear how it goes, and I’m happy to walk your team through it.

You own the product. The framework owns the architecture. The agent builds. Trust the agent, and verify with the build.

  • /next-task: step 6

  • /align and /drift-reset: step 8

title: Director-Driven Development: A New Way of Working with AI Coding Agents
excerpt: Director-Driven Development is a new way of working with AI coding agents: small context, surgical tasks and automated checks. You direct, the AI builds.
content:
Our role as developers in the AI coding assistant world has changed. We no longer write most of the code. We direct it.

A single prompt can build an app. The trouble starts with the second prompt: the fix, the new feature, the change to something that already works. I call it the second prompt problem. That is where results start to vary from session to session. Context fills up and the agent loses track. The design drifts as it quietly decides things nobody agreed to. “Done” means “it compiled”. Every new session reinterprets the project from scratch.

That isn’t a flaw in the model. AI is a non-deterministic tool, and that is also where its creativity comes from. The cause is a codebase and a workflow built for humans. Director-Driven Development is the way of working I built to fix that: creativity, inside a frame. Small context, small tasks, and automated proof that every task works.

The principle

A director doesn’t need to act. A director needs to recognize a good take.

You don’t write the implementation. You decide what gets built, judge the result and own the design. Left alone, an agent makes every prompt work as fast as you ask, and every change looks reasonable on its own. That is exactly how a codebase rots. Someone has to hold the whole picture. That’s the director.

Four roles:

  • Director (you): design, priorities, acceptance. Final say.
  • Orchestrator (main session): picks tasks, records decisions, hands off builds. Never reads the code being changed.
  • Builder: builds one task in a fresh context and reports back.
  • Reviewer: independent, read-only review of every change against its task and the tests.

Code shaped for agents

Agent quality drops as context grows. So the codebase is shaped to keep every task’s context small.

  • Small, separate units. Even a small app becomes a set of internal services and functions. One function per file, and every file works like a small service: input in, output out.
  • Read only what the task needs. Each task names the files it may touch. The builder greps for the exact rows it needs and reads nothing else.
  • Surgical edits. One task, one atomic change, one commit. Large tasks are split before they start.
  • Rules live in testable code. Agents are strong at UI because UI is easy to verify, and weak at complex rules. So rules live in plain classes that tests build directly, and the check fails when the UI holds logic.
  • State lives in files, not chat. A design document, a decision log, a task queue and an architecture table hold everything. Each fact has one home. Clearing the session loses nothing.

The loop

Every change runs the same four steps.

1. Decide

The agent proposes. The director decides. Design calls come to you as 2-4 options with a recommendation, and you can always write your own answer. Only your choice is recorded, in a decision log in the repo, so the next session starts from what was agreed rather than a fresh guess. Anything undecided goes on an open-questions list, and values you haven’t set stay marked as placeholders. The agent never guesses intent.

2. Build

The orchestrator hands one sized task to a builder with a fresh, empty context. The builder returns a short structured report. The orchestrator never reads the changed code, so ten tasks cost about as much context as one.

Each task size maps to its own model: Haiku for XS and S, Sonnet for M, Opus for L and XL, with Fable as an alternative for the largest tasks. A failed build retries once on the next size up. Cost follows complexity, not habit.

3. Prove

One check defines done: the project builds, the tests pass and the architecture rules hold. “It compiled” is not an answer. Large changes, and medium ones that touch contracts, stored data or other risky boundaries, also get an independent, read-only reviewer in a fresh context before they are committed.

4. Commit

A passing check gates every commit. Run a single task and you approve it. Work through the queue and commits land automatically, listed in the final report.

What makes it different

None of the building blocks are new. Small batches, a single source of truth, a definition of done, decision records and an orchestrator delegating to sub-agents are all established practice. In regulated industries we have long run platforms the same way: trust, but verify. Enforce what’s critical, audit the rest. Director-Driven Development combines these for AI agents and adds four things:

  • Rules are enforced, not suggested. Most AI workflows guide the agent with prompts and templates, and prompts can be ignored. Here the check fails the build: a rule inside the UI, a tenant ID read from a request, logic in the wrong layer.
  • Deviation is a decision. Where the framework owns the architecture, the only way past a rule is an architecture decision record the director accepts. The check excuses only the exceptions an accepted record names. Builders and reviewers have limited autonomy: anything they find outside their task is flagged for the director, not fixed on the spot.
  • Context discipline is a rule, not a tip. The orchestrator never reads the code being changed. Its context holds decisions and reports, so a long session stays as sharp as a short one.
  • Ownership is enforced by tools. The director’s own workspace is protected by a hook: the agent can read it, but never write to it. Areas the director owns, like art and audio, get placeholders until they are ready to be replaced with production-ready assets.

When the design drifts

Agents don’t break your design. They drift. Complex rule systems drift in interpretation: a principle that can be read two ways gets read two ways. I handle that at two levels.

Align often. /align is a routine consistency pass. It checks that everything is accounted for: every design rule has a task, every decision is reflected in the design document, every part of the architecture points at something real. Mechanical drift gets fixed; anything that touches the design comes back to the director. When the same conflict comes back, or one conflict spans several design principles, align recommends a reset.

Reset when you have to. Sometimes everything is accounted for, but the same principle has been built two different ways. Don’t patch. Reset. /drift-reset walks the director through it, and only the director can start it:

  1. Analyse the system as built, area by area, with read-only reviewers in fresh contexts.
  2. Map how each design principle was actually interpreted, and where.
  3. Rewrite the design document, one design call at a time. Only the director’s choices are recorded.
  4. Plan the rebuild as ordinary sized tasks. The rebuild itself runs through /next-task.
  5. Run /drift-reset postmortem against the old failure modes. Drift a script could have caught becomes a proposed check rule, for the director to approve.

It means throwing work away. That is the price of keeping the design yours, and the routine align pass is what keeps the price rare.

Three frameworks, one model

All are MIT licensed and run locally. Designed to work with any AI coding assistant that reads AGENTS.md. Built and tested on Claude Code.

  • Godot-Director: games in Godot 4. The check fails if a screen script holds game rules.
  • App-Director: small web, mobile and desktop apps, with TypeScript, Flutter and Python stacks.
  • SaaSAllTheThings: B2B SaaS on Azure. You own the product, the framework owns the architecture, the agent builds. Tenancy, identity and cost rules are machine-checked. Deviation requires an ADR you accept.

The same loop runs all three, and all three ship /align and /drift-reset. Only the rules the check enforces change. Directing scales by turning repeated judgment into checks.

Who it’s for

Anyone who can judge the design of code, even without writing it. You need design judgment, the discipline to keep documents authoritative, and the willingness to throw work away when it no longer matches intent.

AI didn’t remove the need for engineering judgment. It concentrated it.

In the docs
This post is the why. The how, step by step, is in the Director-Driven Development docs.
