  • The three frameworks compared

title: Sovereign Cloud Part 3: Disconnected operations change the sovereignty conversation for Azure Local
excerpt: Disconnected operations shift a critical dependency boundary: operational control no longer collapses when the public control plane disappears.
content:
February 2026 marked a major shift for Azure Local. Disconnected Operations.

With disconnected operations now generally available, Azure Local no longer requires continuous connectivity to the Azure public control plane to operate, govern, or run workloads. This is a major shift and enabler of sovereign operation. In practice, it creates a new responsibility: organizations can and must now design for, test, and rehearse operating without external connectivity.

This article focuses on why disconnected operations matter for sovereignty, what Azure Local actually is, and why customers should treat disconnection as a scenario to actively test rather than a theoretical edge case.

Setting the stage: Sovereignty and Azure Local

In part 2 of this series, an important nuance emerged in the discussion around sovereignty, one that is worth making explicit before going deeper. Shout out to Rickard Carlsson for the discourse 😘.

Even when an organization understands where workloads run, who can administer them, and which regulations apply, a fundamental dependency remains: the platform provider itself.

In public cloud platforms, sovereignty is always bounded by what the provider chooses to expose, document, and allow customers to verify. Customers do not have full insight into internal operational mechanisms, such as internal access paths, key handling implementations, or emergency procedures, unless they fully own or can independently audit the entire platform.

This does not make public cloud insecure or unusable. It simply means sovereignty in the cloud is always, to some extent, a matter of conscious risk acceptance.

As the well-known saying goes: “There is no cloud – it’s just someone else’s computer.” The value of Azure, and other hyperscale platforms, lies in convenience, speed, and access to advanced capabilities that would be unrealistic to build and operate independently. The trade-off is reduced direct control.

What is often overlooked, however, is that this trade-off does not disappear in private datacenters or so-called private clouds.

Even fully private environments are deeply dependent on vendors across the entire value chain: operating systems, hypervisors, licensing models, subscription services, development tooling, identity platforms, and documentation systems. Critical functionality can be gated, altered, or withdrawn through licensing and contractual changes, not only through technical failures. Even going fully into open-source has trade offs in integration complexity, and ultimately raises the TCO for your platform in terms of manpower requirements.

Sovereignty, therefore, is rarely, if ever, absolute.

It is about understanding and deliberately choosing which dependencies are acceptable, and under which conditions they remain acceptable.

Azure Local operates in this space intentionally. It does not claim to eliminate vendor dependency. What it changes is where the operational control boundary sits, and what continues to function when external systems, control planes, or connectivity are no longer available.

This is why disconnected operations matter.

They do not remove all risk. They reduce dependency in the scenarios where dependency matters most.

What Azure Local is and how it differs from traditional on-premises datacenters

Azure Local allows customers to run Azure services in their own datacenters, on hardware they control, while retaining a cloud-native operational and governance model.

This is not traditional virtualization with a cloud management veneer.

Compared to classic on-premises environments, Azure Local provides:

  • Azure-native infrastructure, managed and operated using the same resource model, policies, and identity concepts as Azure.
  • A consistent governance and security model across local, hybrid, and cloud environments.
  • The ability to deploy IaaS, PaaS, and selected SaaS-like services locally, not just virtual machines.

The key difference is not physical location. It is operational alignment.

Traditional datacenters require separate tooling, separate governance models, and often separate teams. Azure Local allows organizations to extend their Azure governance and operating model into their own facilities, reducing divergence while maintaining physical and legal control.

Until recently, however, there was a critical limitation.

What changed in February 2026: Disconnected operations

As of early 2026, Azure Local supports full disconnected operations.

This means:

  • No runtime dependency on the Azure public control plane.
  • No outbound connectivity required for infrastructure or governance.
  • No customer data leaving the environment.
  • Management, policy enforcement, and operations continue locally.

This matters because sovereignty has always struggled with a simple question:

What happens if connectivity is lost, restricted, or intentionally removed?

Disconnected operations answer that question directly.

Infrastructure, governance, and now AI workloads can continue to operate entirely within the customer’s sovereign boundary. Control does not degrade when connectivity disappears.

This is a significant change from earlier hybrid models where loss of connectivity often meant loss of control.

AI in disconnected environments: Completing the sovereign stack

Another important development is the expansion of Foundry Local.

Foundry Local now supports large, enterprise-grade AI models in disconnected environments. Not only small edge models, but multimodal models capable of meaningful inference workloads.

Crucially:

  • Models, prompts, and inference results remain local.
  • No prompts or metadata are sent externally.
  • AI can run close to sensitive, regulated, or operational data.

For many organizations, this removes a major blocker.

Customers that previously could not use AI due to sovereignty, data protection, or control plane dependency concerns can now do so without introducing external reliance.

At this point, the sovereign private cloud stack becomes complete:

  • Infrastructure runs locally.
  • Governance is enforced locally.
  • Productivity and AI workloads operate locally.
  • No runtime dependency on public cloud services.

What disconnected means in practice

Disconnected operations are not only about air-gapped military environments. They are relevant whenever reliance on external control planes is unacceptable.

Typical scenarios include:

  • Intentionally isolated or restricted environments.
  • Security policies that forbid dependency on public control planes.
  • AI workloads handling sensitive or classified data.
  • Mission-critical systems that must continue through prolonged network outages.
  • Environments with extreme latency requirements or near real-time control systems.

From a sovereignty perspective, this changes the dependency question.

The organization can now clearly answer what it depends on to keep running. That answer no longer includes continuous access to the public cloud.

Why fire drills matter

Disconnected capability is only sovereign if it is proven.

Too many organizations assume disconnection “would probably work” without ever testing it. Sovereignty fails in the gap between theory and reality.

Fire drills should be mandatory.

Organizations using Azure Local in a sovereign context should intentionally test:

  • Loss of all outbound connectivity.
  • Extended operation in fully disconnected mode.
  • Recovery, updates, and governance enforcement without cloud access.
  • Operational readiness of staff when cloud backstops are unavailable.

If disconnected operations only exist on a slide, sovereignty is assumed, not enforced.

Relevance for Swedish and European customers

In Sweden and across the EU, sovereignty requirements are becoming stricter, not looser.

Regulatory frameworks such as EDPB guidance, DORA, NIS2, and sector-specific requirements increasingly require:

  • Clear control boundaries.
  • Evidence of operational independence.
  • Reduced reliance on foreign jurisdictions for critical systems.

Azure Local with disconnected operations does not eliminate all trust considerations. Microsoft is still a vendor. Software supply chains still matter.

What it does provide is the ability for the customer to retain operational control even when trust is questioned, connectivity is lost, or conditions change.

That distinction is increasingly important.

For decision makers and the owners of corporate IT capabilities and platforms

Disconnected Azure Local is particularly relevant when you say or hear statements like:

  • “Data must not leave Sweden.”
  • “The environment must not be connected.”
  • “We cannot rely on public AI services.”
  • “AI must not send prompts or metadata externally.”
  • “We need modern capabilities without cloud dependency.”

These are not edge cases. They are becoming mainstream requirements in public sector, critical infrastructure, and regulated industries.

Closing thoughts

Sovereignty is not about eliminating all dependency. That has never been realistic.

It is about understanding dependencies, choosing them deliberately, and ensuring that control holds when conditions are no longer ideal.

Disconnected operations in Azure Local do not claim to make environments magically independent of vendors, software supply chains, or commercial relationships. What they do is shift a critical dependency boundary. Operational control no longer collapses when connectivity to a public control plane disappears.

That shift matters for organizations where availability, trust, jurisdiction, or accountability cannot be conditional.

The real value of disconnected Azure Local is therefore not the feature itself, but what it forces organizations to confront: what they actually depend on to keep running, and whether those dependencies are acceptable under stress.

Sovereignty is never proven in architecture diagrams or procurement slides. It is proven when assumptions fail.

If sovereignty matters to you, treat disconnection as a first class scenario. Test it deliberately. Operate through it. Learn from it.

Anything less is trust by assumption, not control by design.

Originally published on LinkedIn on April 22, 2026.

title: Sovereign Cloud Part 2: The technical controls that make sovereignty real in a public cloud
excerpt: Sovereign cloud is not defined by a list of security features, but by whether control is enforceable under adverse conditions.
content:
Part 1: What sovereignty actually means in the public cloud

This article is a continuation on my previous article where I talk about Sovreignty, what it is and why it matters. In part 2 I want to focus on the actual controls that can grant Sovreignty in Public Cloud

“Sovereign cloud” can not be defined by a list of security features enabled, but it is instead defined by whether control is enforceable under adverse conditions such as (but not limited to) misconfiguration, insider threat, and privileged access scenarios. For any Cloud or PaaS/SaaS service this includes validating if the control is enforceable against the Service Providers themselves (Scary, I know).

The Sovereign Cloud Technical Control Matrix

Think of a Sovereign Cloud Technical Control Matrix as a structured way to answer:

  • Which controls exist, and what scope they cover
  • How they are enforced (deny, allow with conditions, audit)
  • How exceptions work, who can grant them, for how long, and with what auditable evidence
  • How controls interact so you are not betting sovereignty on a single layer

Sovereignty is measured by what, and when the platform can actually technically prevent or cryptographically invalidate (hard controls). Not by user processes, intent, guidance, or documentation (soft controls).

How sovereign controls work together (layered enforcement)

Sovereign posture in a public cloud comes from controls reinforcing each other across layers:

Identity and access controls

These controls answer: who can change or access what, and under which conditions.

A sovereign posture generally requires:

  • No standing high privilege access for day-to-day work
  • Time-bound, approval-based elevation for privileged roles
  • Clear separation between different types of privilege:
    • Control plane operations (platform configuration)
    • Data plane access (reading or operating on data)
    • Security operations (security tooling and alerts)
  • Separation of duties across privileged workflows, so no individual can act as judge, jury, and executioner for high-impact actions or privileged access.

I know it might seem tedious to enforce these things, as an operator/administrator this can be felt like an administrative overhead, but these things should be non-negotiable. In physical security we treat every warehouse and store-room with high value objects using access-card locks, we monitor, we place patrolling guards around the perimiter and inside the areas. We delegate access to employees on a strict need-only basis.

If we don’t treat our IT systems with the same respect in terms of access, then it’s not a question about if an incident occurs it’s a question of when, and how often and how much does it cost.

These controls is how you avoid a single account obtaining a “master key” without supervision or restraint.

Policy controls

These controls answer: what can exist in your environment.

If sovereignty depends on reviews and guidance, it is still trust-based.

A sovereign baseline relies on policy that can:

  • Deny non-compliant deployments by default
  • Continuously evaluate services for drift or non-compliance
  • Require exemptions to be time-bound and auditable

Network controls

These controls answer: where data is allowed to flow.

A sovereign posture typically needs:

  • Centrally governed ingress patterns for anything exposed publicly
  • Centrally governed egress controls so data cannot leave through unapproved paths
  • Controls that limit lateral movement between workloads and services

The goal is simple: even authorized identities should not be able to bypass the approved architecture.

Cryptographic controls

These controls answer: what happens if access controls are bypassed.

Cryptography is the final enforcement layer because it can make data unusable even if someone gains access.

For sovereignty, the important part is not “encryption exists”. The important part is who controls the keys, and whether the customer can:

  • Rotate keys
  • Disable keys
  • Destroy keys in a way that renders data cryptographically inaccessible

Logging and monitoring controls

These controls answer: can you prove what happened.

Sovereignty needs evidence:

  • Privileged actions must be attributable
  • Changes must be traceable to an identity, a ticket/approval, and a time window
  • Alerts must exist for sovereign boundary violations, not just availability issues

Without evidence, you do not have accountability. You have claims.

What “good” looks like: the sovereignty litmus test

A platform is not sovereign-ready for workload onboarding if any of these are true.

Access control

  • Privileged access cannot be fully revoked or time-bounded without changing application code or workload configuration.
  • Administrative access relies on standing permissions rather than just-in-time elevation with enforced approval and logging.

Cryptographic control

  • The customer does not retain exclusive control over encryption keys protecting data at rest.
  • Data confidentiality depends solely on access controls rather than cryptographic enforcement.

Data residency

  • Data location is governed by convention or documentation rather than enforceable technical controls.
  • The platform cannot prevent replication, backup, or processing outside approved regions.

Network and service exposure

  • Public endpoint exposure can be enabled without an explicit centrally enforced control mechanism.
  • Platform teams cannot centrally restrict egress paths and service-to-service communication.

Policy enforcement

  • Compliance depends on reviews or manual approvals rather than deny-by-default policy enforcement.
  • Deviations from the sovereign baseline are not time-bound, tracked, and auditable.

If any of these conditions exist, the platform may be well secured, but it does not provide sovereign assurance.

The operational reality behind “toxic combinations”

Even with a strong sovereign architecture and the right technical controls in place, there is often a limiting factor that determines whether sovereignty actually holds in practice.

That factor is people and organization.

Technical controls can enforce boundaries, but they do not operate themselves. A sovereign posture depends on having highly qualified engineers covering distinct areas of responsibility, without overlap of duties that would undermine those controls.

This is where the concept often referred to as a “toxic combination” becomes critical.

Why toxic combinations matter

A toxic combination exists when the same individuals can both:

  • grant themselves access to workloads or storage, and
  • access, modify, or disable the encryption keys protecting that data.

When this happens, sovereignty no longer rests on enforceable control. It collapses into trust in individuals.

No matter how strong the technical platform is, if one person or one team can act unilaterally across control, access, and protection, the system is no longer sovereign in any meaningful sense.

What a sovereign operating model requires

In a sovereign design, responsibilities must be deliberately separated and staffed by different roles with no practical ability to override each other:

  • Platform operators can build, run, and maintain the platform, but cannot decrypt or access data.
  • Key administrators can control cryptographic keys, but cannot grant themselves access to workloads or data.
  • Security operators can monitor, investigate, and enforce response, but do not operate workloads or manage keys.

This separation is not theoretical. It is an operational safeguard designed to ensure that no single role becomes all-powerful.

If an exception is required where an individual must temporarily assume a toxic combination of privileges, that elevation must be governed by a formal process requiring explicit approval, full traceability, and continuous monitoring. All actions performed under such elevation must be independently audited to ensure accountability.

Why people matter as much as controls

For this model to work, organizations must invest in:

  • sufficiently skilled engineers in each domain,
  • clear role definitions and responsibility boundaries,
  • staffing models that avoid role concentration out of convenience or cost.

Sovereignty fails quietly when organizations collapse roles “temporarily” or “for efficiency”. Those shortcuts are rarely reversed, and they erode control faster than any technical misconfiguration.

From technical sovereignty to operational sovereignty

True sovereignty is not achieved when controls exist. It is achieved when they are:

  • operated by different people,
  • continuously monitored,
  • independently auditable.

In regulated environments, this is why external oversight matters. Regulatory institutions, auditors, and supervisory authorities play a critical role in verifying that sovereignty is not just declared in architecture diagrams, but upheld in day-to-day operations.

Sovereignty is therefore not only a technical posture. It is an operational discipline, sustained by people, process, and scrutiny over time.

Concrete control areas for Azure public cloud

The controls for Azure Platforms can be summarised as follows. Keep in mind that these controls might not be complete, as there is no peer-review on this article, and this is written using a point in time (early 2026) and the security landscape is ever evolving and expanding.

Identity and access (Entra ID)

  • Centralized tenant governance for identity, conditional access, and privileged workflows
  • No standing privileged access for administrators
  • Break-glass accounts defined, tested, and monitored
  • Privileged Identity Management for time-bound elevation (approval + logging)
  • Custom RBAC roles for consumers with explicit denial of sensitive platform actions
  • Separation of duties between control plane, data plane, and security operations

Management group and subscription topology

  • A management group hierarchy that supports consistent enforcement
  • Clear ownership boundaries between platform and consumer scopes
  • A rule that platform consumers cannot assign roles or policies which override governance policies.

Policy baseline (deny-by-default)

  • Allowed locations, enforced
  • Allowed services, enforced
  • Network architecture requirements, enforced
  • Encryption requirements where supported (prefer customer-managed keys for sensitive data)
  • Exemptions that are time-bound, tracked, and auditable
  • Policy changes via version-controlled code and peer review

Network boundary controls

  • Approved ingress patterns (and no “click-to-public” endpoints without governance)
  • Central egress restrictions and service-to-service controls
  • Mandatory monitoring for boundary violations

Cryptography and key control

  • Customer-controlled keys for sensitive data, with the ability to disable or destroy keys
  • Operational separation between key administrators and platform administrators
  • Evidence that key access is approved, time-bound, and logged

Evidence and auditability

  • Logs bound to identity, time, and approval context
  • Monitoring that detects both configuration drift and boundary violations
  • Reporting that supports audits without relying on verbal assurance

Why this matters right now in Europe

Sovereignty requirements in Sweden and the EU are increasingly shaped by an uncomfortable reality: many organizations must assume distrust.

Even if you use the big public cloud providers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google) with EU data residency, the provider is still a company under foreign sovereignty. That pushes buyers toward controls that are enforceable and provable, not promises.

The controls outlined in this article apply equally to local private cloud providers and privately operated datacenters. Sovereignty is defined by control, not proximity. If effective control cannot be exercised, sovereignty does not exist.

In a later part, I will explore private cloud sovereignty and Azure Local with Disconnected Operations, and why the ability to operate without reliance on public cloud control planes is becoming a real requirement for certain organizations and workloads.

Originally published on LinkedIn on March 20, 2026.

title: What sovereignty actually means in the public cloud
excerpt: Sovereignty is not primarily about where data sits. It is about control and accountability.
content:
When people talk about sovereignty in the cloud, the conversation almost always starts with geography.

When discussing this we often hear “Does our data stay in Sweden?” or “Is it stored inside the EU?”. These are reasonable questions. They are just not the full story.

Sovereignty is not primarily about where data sits. It is about control and accountability.

For organizations consuming cloud services, sovereignty is the ability to clearly answer three basic questions.

The three questions that define sovereignty

  1. Who is in control of the data and the systems? Who ultimately decides how systems are configured, operated, changed, or shut down.
  2. Who can access or operate them, and under which laws? Who has technical access, operational authority, or legal reach if something goes wrong.
  3. What does the business depend on to keep running? Which external services, networks, or decisions must exist for operations to continue.

If these questions cannot be answered clearly, sovereignty is assumed rather than understood.

Why location alone is not enough

It is entirely possible for data to be physically stored in Sweden or elsewhere in the EU and still not be sovereign in practice.

Data location alone does not automatically answer:

  • Who can technically access the systems
  • Who operates and maintains the platform
  • Which laws apply to operators and vendors
  • What happens if connectivity, services, or support is disrupted

Sovereignty is about control under real conditions, not just during normal operations.

The trust question in Europe

In Sweden and across the EU, sovereignty discussions are increasingly shaped by a broader trust issue.

Microsoft, Amazon, and Google are all US-based companies. Regardless of where data is stored, these providers themselves operate under a foreign legal and political sovereignty.

This creates understandable concern for public sector organizations and regulated industries:

  • What legal obligations apply to the provider if a foreign authority makes a request?
  • What happens if geopolitical conditions change?
  • What level of dependency is acceptable for critical systems?

For many decision-makers, the concern is not technical. It is institutional and legal.

An example

Consider a Swedish public authority using a public cloud service.

The data may be stored in an EU datacenter. Access may be restricted. Encryption may be strong.

But if:

  • The control plane is operated from outside the EU
  • Platform operations depend on continuous connectivity to global services
  • Support, updates, or security decisions are made under foreign jurisdiction

Then sovereignty becomes conditional.

The question is no longer “Where is the data?” It becomes “Who is in control if something happens?”

What sovereignty means in public cloud terms

In a public cloud, sovereignty does not mean that no external provider is involved. It means understanding and actively managing the relationship with that provider.

In practical terms, public cloud sovereignty is about:

  • Transparency around roles and responsibilities
  • Clear boundaries for access and operations
  • Legal clarity around jurisdiction and accountability
  • Awareness of operational dependencies

You are not asking: “Is this cloud foreign or local?”

You are asking: “Who can do what, under which conditions, and what do we depend on?”

The questions non-technical leaders should ask

Sovereignty is not an IT problem. It is a governance problem.

Non-technical leaders should be asking:

  • If there is a crisis, who has the authority and technical capabilities to act on our systems?
  • If connectivity is lost, what continues to work and what stops?
  • If regulations change, do we have options or are we locked in?
  • If trust is questioned, can we prove who controls what?

These are business questions. They just happen to involve cloud services.

Sovereignty is a spectrum, not a switch

A common misconception is that sovereignty is binary. Either you have it or you do not. In reality, sovereignty exists on a spectrum.

Different workloads require different levels of control:

  • Some can operate with shared responsibility and external dependencies
  • Others require tighter operational, legal, or physical control
  • Some must continue running even if disconnected or intentionally isolated

Understanding sovereignty means understanding which level of control is appropriate where.

Setting the stage

This article is the first part of a series.

The purpose here is to establish a shared understanding:

  • Sovereignty is about control, accountability, and dependency
  • It applies to public cloud usage, not just private environments
  • It is a business concern first, and a technical concern second

In the next part, the focus will go into details on the technical controls that make sovereignty real in a public clouds

title: DevOps & Rocket manufacturing
excerpt: Elon Musk’s 5 steps to building rockets apply to just about any process in any industry, including IT and DevOps.
content:
I was catching up on one of my favourite youtube channels (Everyday Astronaut) during my morning coffee. The video is a SpaceX tour with Elon Musk and basically from nowhere Elon Musk starts to describe DevOps processes and how they apply to SpaceX design process and production line.

He describes 5 steps to building rockets, but this can be implemented to just about any process in any industry. I have paraphrased the steps and taken the liberty to expand on some steps in order to apply to the industry I’m working in.

  1. Make your requirements less dumb. – “Your requirements are definitely dumb. It does not matter who gave the requirements. It’s particularly dangerous if a smart person defined the requirements”.
  2. Delete the part or process step – For IT the parts are often an infrastructure component or a part of an application (function, microservices etc.). Run tight margins on what makes it into the product. Any part or process that is not critical should be added to a backlog and re-added when needed. Build a MVP (minimum viable product), only add what you need and focus on what matters without over-engineering. Another take-away from this is that requirements and constraints must be owned by a person and never a department. You can’t ask a department why a requirement or constraint is in place since people move around or leave the organization. Design decisions, processes and products should have ownership of an individual. If we trace back to a department we might loose the detailed how and why of a part or process. Review all parts of the process, and remove what does not fit the requirements.
  3. Simplify or Optimize – “It’s very common of a smart engineer is to optimize something that should not exist”. Focus on your requirements before working on optimizing.
  4. Accelerate cycle time – “You’re moving too slowly, go faster.” But don’t go faster unless you have cycled through the first three steps. Focus on the constraining process in your delivery chain, if it is a manual process or an automated build/release process you can always go faster
  5. Automate, but only when step 1-4 are cycled through. We often go in the opposite direction. We often automate or fix the automation before we fix the process. I can attest that as a self-proclaimed automation aficionado I stumble down this rabbit hole a bit too often. Automate the part or process you have identified as the most impactful part/constraint of your delivery chain. When you’re done revert back to step 1 and work your way through the process again.

These five steps are so intuitive when read as listed above, but often extremely difficult to apply when in the middle of a project.

Now, how is this related to DevOps? What Elon is listing is a process that can be directly linked to several core concepts in DevOps, and most importantly the “three ways”.

Work always flows in one direction – Downstream. Focus on what matters and don’t optimize downstream. The concept “shift-left” is often cited here. – The process of never optimizing at the end

Create, shorten and amplify feedback loops. Here we often talk about failing fast – The process of segmenting a product into small manageable chunks that can be developed, tested, deployed and re-iterated upon without having to rebuild the whole project before testing

Continued experimentation, in order to learn from mistakes, and achive mastery. In Elon Musks 5 steps, this is highly related to his 2nd step, where we always review and re-iterate on our needs and create a mindset focused on our requirements and how to approach them. When we have a good requirement we go forward with the process of developing, optimizing and automating. I also belive that their success is part of how many rockets they launch, get telemetry and improve. Even when the rockets experience “rapid unscheduled disassembly” SpaceX considers this a success because it gaves them opportunies for destructive testing (DT).

Enough of my ramblings, check out the full video! The link to get directly to the 5 steps lecture.

https://youtu.be/t705r8ICkRw?t=814

content:
Reblogged from my company blog: https://tech.xenit.se/just-enough-administration-rds/
—

The Problem?

Microsoft RDS has limitations when delegating access, in fact there is no built-in access delegation whatsoever!

The solution? Powershell!

A Just enough Administration (JEA) endpoint, also known as a Constrained Powershell Endpoint.
The endpoint is restricted to only access List collection, list users and subsequently force logoff users. The endpoint configuration to only accept users from a certain AD group.

To configure endpoint, run the following code on all connection brokers. The script is somewhat generalized for easy adaptability. The main parts are in the parameters where we configure who can run, using which account and also what cmdlet are available in the constrained session.

<#
.Synopsis
    Short description
.DESCRIPTION
    
.NOTES
    Name: Create-JEA-RDS-Endpoint.ps1
    Author: Vikingur Saemundsson
    Date Created: 2017-11-20
    Version History:
        2017-11-20 - Vikingur Saemundsson
            Initial Creation

    Xenit AB
#>

[cmdletbinding()]
Param(
    [String]$Name = 'Xenit.JEA.RDS.Servicedesk',
    [String]$Path = 'C:\Xenit\RDS\LogoffEndpoint',
    [Array]$VisibleCmdlets = $("Get-RDSessionCollection","Get-RDSessionHost","Get-RDUserSession","Invoke-RDUserLogoff","Where-object"),
    [String]$AdGroup = 'Servicedesk Ad group',
    [Parameter(Mandatory=$true)]
    [String]$ServiceAccount,
    [Array]$Modules = 'RemoteDesktop',
    [String]$Author = 'Vikingur Saemundsson',
    [String]$Company = 'Xenit AB'
)
Try{
    $ADGroupSID = (Get-ADGroup $AdGroup).SID

    If(-not(Test-Path -Path $Path -PathType Container)){
        New-Item -Path $Path -ItemType Directory -Force
    }

    $LockdownScript = @'
    Get-Command | Where Visibility -eq 'Public' | ForEach-Object {
        if ( $_.Name -notin $CmdsToExclude ) {
            $_.Visibility = 'Private'
        }
    }
'@ 
    '$CmdsToExclude = @("Get-Command", "Out-Default", "Exit-PSSession", "Measure-Object", "Select-Object" , "Get-FormatData"{0})' -f (($VisibleCmdlets | ForEach-Object{",`"$_`""}) -join '') | Out-File "$Path\LockdownScript.ps1"
    $LockdownScript | Out-File "$Path\LockdownScript.ps1" -Append

    $Modules += 'Microsoft.PowerShell.Core'
    $Modules += 'Microsoft.PowerShell.Management'
    $Modules += 'Microsoft.PowerShell.Security'
    $Modules += 'Microsoft.PowerShell.Utility'
    $Modules += 'Microsoft.PowerShell.Diagnostics'
    $Modules += 'Microsoft.PowerShell.Host'

    $ConfigFileParams = @{
        Path ="$Path\$Name.pssc"
        ModulesToImport = $Modules
        ScriptsToProcess = "$Path\LockdownScript.ps1"
        CompanyName = $Company
        Author = $Author
        Copyright = "(c) $((Get-Date).Year) $Company. All rights reserved."
        SessionType = 'Default'
        LanguageMode = "ConstrainedLanguage"
        ExecutionPolicy = 'Bypass'
    }

    $SessionConfigParams = @{
        RunAsCredential = $ServiceAccount
        Name = $Name
        Path = $ConfigFileParams.Path
        UseSharedProcess = $true
        SecurityDescriptorSddl = "O:BAG:DUD:AI(A;;GX;;;$ADGroupSID)"
        Confirm = $false
    }

    If(Get-PSSessionConfiguration -Name $SessionConfigParams.Name -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue){
        Unregister-PSSessionConfiguration -Name $SessionConfigParams.Name -Confirm:$false
    }

    New-PSSessionConfigurationFile @ConfigFileParams

    Register-PSSessionConfiguration @SessionConfigParams
}
Catch{
    Write-Error $_
}

The frontend application code is not posted in the blog.

content:
Reblogged from my company blog: https://tech.xenit.se/recursively-search-azure-ad-group-members/
—
When working with on-premise Active Directory an administrator often has to recursively search AD groups, this is easy using the ActiveDirectory module with cmdlet “Get-AdGroupMember <Group> -Recusive”.
For the AzureAD equivalent this is no longer an option, the cmdlet Get-AzureADGroupMember has three parameters.

PARAMETERS
-All <Boolean>
If true, return all group members. If false, return the number of objects specified by the Top parameter
-ObjectId <String>
Specifies the ID of a group in Azure AD.
-Top <Int32>
Specifies the maximum number of records to return.

As we can see there is no -recursive, in order to search recursively I’ve written the function below.

Function Get-RecursiveAzureAdGroupMemberUsers{
[cmdletbinding()]
param(
   [parameter(Mandatory=$True,ValueFromPipeline=$true)]
   $AzureGroup
)
    Begin{
        If(-not(Get-AzureADCurrentSessionInfo)){Connect-AzureAD}
    }
    Process {
        Write-Verbose -Message "Enumerating $($AzureGroup.DisplayName)"
        $Members = Get-AzureADGroupMember -ObjectId $AzureGroup.ObjectId -All $true
        
        $UserMembers = $Members | Where-Object{$_.ObjectType -eq 'User'}
        If($Members | Where-Object{$_.ObjectType -eq 'Group'}){
            $UserMembers += $Members | Where-Object{$_.ObjectType -eq 'Group'} | ForEach-Object{ Get-RecursiveAzureAdGroupMemberUsers -AzureGroup $_}
        }
    }
    end {
        Return $UserMembers
    }
}

The function accepts groups by parameter or by pipeline and returns only the object type ‘User’

To run a recursive AzureAD Group member search simply pipe a normal ADgroup search as below

Get-AzureADGroup -SearchString 'AzureADGroupName' | Get-RecursiveAzureAdGroupMemberUsers

content:
Reblogged from my company blog: https://tech.xenit.se/azure-automation-running-scripts-locally-vm-runbooks/
—
I was tasked to create a powershell script to run on a schedule on a Azure VM. Normally this would be running as a scheduled task on the VM but seeing as we’re working with AzureVM and schedule tasks are legacy I wanted to explore the possibilities of running the schedule and script in Azure to keep the VM clean and the configuration scalable.

After some research the best option would be running the powershell script as a CustomScriptExtension on the VM, and the schedule would be handled by a Process Automation Runbook (using Automation Accounts).

What I ended up with is the script below. It’s fairly easy to configure and contains almost all the required configuration in the parameters.

How does it work? Simple!

Prerequisites

  1. Create a Storage Account
    • Create a Private Blob container
  2. Create a Automation Account
    • Make sure a RunAsAccount is created

Runbook configuration

  1. Navigate to the Automation Account you intend to use
  2. Create a Powershell runbook and press Edit
  3. Copy the below script into the runbook and save
    • Fill out the parameters with relevant information (subscription, resourcegroup etc)
    • Make sure to set the name of the StorageContainer to the one where you want to host the scripts
    • Extension name should be unique for the job, as well as the ScriptName
    • The scriptblock parameter takes the script you intend to run on the VMs
  4. On the first run, go into the Test Pane from edit view and edit the UploadScript parameter to $True
    • This will make the runbook actually save the script to the Container, allowing the VM download and run the script
  5. Done!

Now simply register schedules to the runbook. If you want to run the script on several VM you have two options. Either specify multiple VM when creating schedules or create a schedule per machine you want to run the script against.

[cmdletbinding()]
Param(
    $SubscriptionID = '<SubscriptionID>',
    $ResourceGroup = 'RG-NorthEU',
    $VMNames = @('vmname1','vmname2'),
    $StorageAccount = '<StorageAccount>',
    $StorageAccountKey = '<Storagekey>',
    $StorageContainer = 'sc-scripts', # Create this manually before first execution!
    $ExtensionName = 'Xenit.<job>',
    $ScriptName = 'scriptname.ps1',
    
    $UploadScript = $false,
    $ScriptBlock = {
        <Script to run locally on VMs>
    }
)


################
################
#
# DO NOT CHANGE BELOW
#
################
################

function Invoke-AzureRmVmScript {
<#
    
    # Vikingur Saemundsson @ Xenit AB
    # Credit to source https://github.com/RamblingCookieMonster/PowerShell/blob/master/Invoke-AzureRmVmScript.ps1
    # Made som small modifications to allow control over if the scriptfile is uploaded or not to avoid extra data to containers and shorten the executiontime
    #

    .FUNCTIONALITY
        Azure
#>
    [cmdletbinding()]
    param(
        # todo: add various parameter niceties
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $True,
                    Position = 0,
                    ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName = $True)]
        [string[]]$ResourceGroupName,
        
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $True,
                    Position = 1,
                    ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName = $True)]
        [string[]]$VMName,
        
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $True,
                    Position = 2)]
        [scriptblock]$ScriptBlock, #todo: add file support.
        
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $True,
                    Position = 3)]
        [string]$StorageAccountName,

        [string]$StorageAccountKey, #Maybe don't use string...

        $StorageContext,
        
        [string]$StorageContainer = 'sc-scripts',
        
        [string]$Filename, # Auto defined if not specified...
        
        [string]$ExtensionName, # Auto defined if not specified

        [bool]$UploadScript = $true,

        [switch]$ForceExtension,
        [switch]$ForceBlob,
        [switch]$Force
    )
    begin
    {
        if($Force)
        {
            $ForceExtension = $True
            $ForceBlob = $True
        }
    }
    process
    {
        Foreach($ResourceGroup in $ResourceGroupName)
        {
            Foreach($VM in $VMName)
            {
                if(-not $Filename)
                {
                    $GUID = [GUID]::NewGuid().Guid -replace "-", "_"
                    $FileName = "$GUID.ps1"
                }
                if(-not $ExtensionName)
                {
                    $ExtensionName = $Filename -replace '.ps1', ''
                }

                $CommonParams = @{
                    ResourceGroupName = $ResourceGroup
                    VMName = $VM
                }

                Write-Verbose "Working with ResourceGroup $ResourceGroup, VM $VM"
                # Why would Get-AzureRMVmCustomScriptExtension support listing extensions regardless of name? /grumble
                Try
                {
                    $AzureRmVM = Get-AzureRmVM @CommonParams -ErrorAction Stop
                    $AzureRmVMExtended = Get-AzureRmVM @CommonParams -Status -ErrorAction Stop
                }
                Catch
                {
                    Write-Error $_
                    Write-Error "Failed to retrieve existing extension data for $VM"
                    continue
                }

                # Handle existing extensions
                Write-Verbose "Checking for existing extensions on VM '$VM' in resource group '$ResourceGroup'"
                $Extensions = $null
                $Extensions = @( $AzureRmVMExtended.Extensions | Where {$_.Type -like 'Microsoft.Compute.CustomScriptExtension'} )
                if($Extensions.count -gt 0)
                {
                    Write-Verbose "Found extensions on $VM`:`n$($Extensions | Format-List | Out-String)"
                    if(-not $ForceExtension)
                    {
                        Write-Warning "Found CustomScriptExtension '$($Extensions.Name)' on VM '$VM' in Resource Group '$ResourceGroup'.`n Use -ForceExtension or -Force to remove this"
                        continue
                    }
                    Try
                    {
                        # Theoretically can only be one, so... no looping, just remove.
                        $Output = Remove-AzureRmVMCustomScriptExtension @CommonParams -Name $Extensions.Name -Force -ErrorAction Stop
                        if($Output.StatusCode -notlike 'OK')
                        {
                            Throw "Remove-AzureRmVMCustomScriptExtension output seems off:`n$($Output | Format-List | Out-String)"
                        }
                    }
                    Catch
                    {
                        Write-Error $_
                        Write-Error "Failed to remove existing extension $($Extensions.Name) for VM '$VM' in ResourceGroup '$ResourceGroup'"
                        continue
                    }
                }
                
                if(-not $StorageContainer)
                {
                    $StorageContainer = 'scripts'
                }
                if(-not $Filename)
                {
                    $Filename = 'CustomScriptExtension.ps1'
                }
                if(-not $StorageContext)
                {
                    if(-not $StorageAccountKey)
                    {
                        Try
                        {
                            $StorageAccountKey = (Get-AzureRmStorageAccountKey -ResourceGroupName $ResourceGroup -Name $storageAccountName -ErrorAction Stop)[0].value
                        }
                        Catch
                        {
                            Write-Error $_
                            Write-Error "Failed to obtain Storage Account Key for storage account '$StorageAccountName' in Resource Group '$ResourceGroup' for VM '$VM'"
                            continue
                        }
                    }
                    Try
                    {
                        $StorageContext = New-AzureStorageContext -StorageAccountName $StorageAccountName -StorageAccountKey $StorageAccountKey
                    }
                    Catch
                    {
                        Write-Error $_
                        Write-Error "Failed to generate storage context for storage account '$StorageAccountName' in Resource Group '$ResourceGroup' for VM '$VM'"
                        continue
                    }
                }
                If($UploadScript){
                    Write-Verbose "Uploading script to storage account $StorageAccountName"
                    Try
                    {
                        $Script = $ScriptBlock.ToString()
                        $LocalFile = [System.IO.Path]::GetTempFileName()
                        Start-Sleep -Milliseconds 500 #This might not be needed
                        Set-Content $LocalFile -Value $Script -ErrorAction Stop
            
                        $params = @{
                            Container = $StorageContainer
                            Context = $StorageContext
                        }

                        $Existing = $Null
                        $Existing = @( Get-AzureStorageBlob @params -ErrorAction Stop )

                        if($Existing.Name -contains $Filename -and -not $ForceBlob)
                        {
                            Write-Warning "Found blob '$FileName' in container '$StorageContainer'.`n Use -ForceBlob or -Force to overwrite this"
                            continue
                        }
                        $Output = Set-AzureStorageBlobContent @params -File $Localfile -Blob $Filename -ErrorAction Stop -Force
                        if($Output.Name -notlike $Filename)
                        {
                            Throw "Set-AzureStorageBlobContent output seems off:`n$($Output | Format-List | Out-String)"
                        }
                    }
                    Catch
                    {
                        Write-Error $_
                        Write-Error "Failed to generate or upload local script for VM '$VM' in Resource Group '$ResourceGroup'"
                        continue
                    }
                }

                # We have a script in place, set up an extension!
                Write-Verbose "Adding CustomScriptExtension to VM '$VM' in resource group '$ResourceGroup'"
                Try
                {
                    $Output = Set-AzureRmVMCustomScriptExtension -ResourceGroupName $ResourceGroup `
                                                                    -VMName $VM `
                                                                    -Location $AzureRmVM.Location `
                                                                    -FileName $Filename `
                                                                    -Run $Filename `
                                                                    -ContainerName $StorageContainer `
                                                                    -StorageAccountName $StorageAccountName `
                                                                    -StorageAccountKey $StorageAccountKey `
                                                                    -Name $ExtensionName `
                                                                    -TypeHandlerVersion 1.1 `
                                                                    -ErrorAction Stop

                    if($Output.StatusCode -notlike 'OK')
                    {
                        Throw "Set-AzureRmVMCustomScriptExtension output seems off:`n$($Output | Format-List | Out-String)"
                    }
                }
                Catch
                {
                    Write-Error $_
                    Write-Error "Failed to set CustomScriptExtension for VM '$VM' in resource group $ResourceGroup"
                    continue
                }

                # collect the output!
                Try
                {
                    $AzureRmVmOutput = $null
                    $AzureRmVmOutput = Get-AzureRmVM @CommonParams -Status -ErrorAction Stop
                    $SubStatuses = ($AzureRmVmOutput.Extensions | Where {$_.name -like $ExtensionName} ).substatuses
                }
                Catch
                {
                    Write-Error $_
                    Write-Error "Failed to retrieve script output data for $VM"
                    continue
                }

                $Output = [ordered]@{
                    ResourceGroupName = $ResourceGroup
                    VMName = $VM
                    Substatuses = $SubStatuses
                }

                foreach($Substatus in $SubStatuses)
                {
                    $ThisCode = $Substatus.Code -replace 'ComponentStatus/', '' -replace '/', '_'
                    $Output.add($ThisCode, $Substatus.Message)
                }

                [pscustomobject]$Output
            }
        }
    }
}
Try{
    #region Connection to Azure
    write-verbose "Connecting to Azure"
    $connectionName = "AzureRunAsConnection"

    try
    {
        # Get the connection "AzureRunAsConnection "
        $servicePrincipalConnection = Get-AutomationConnection -Name $connectionName         

        "Logging in to Azure..."
        Add-AzureRmAccount `
            -ServicePrincipal `
            -TenantId $servicePrincipalConnection.TenantId `
            -ApplicationId $servicePrincipalConnection.ApplicationId `
            -CertificateThumbprint $servicePrincipalConnection.CertificateThumbprint 
    }
    catch {
        if (!$servicePrincipalConnection)
        {
            $ErrorMessage = "Connection $connectionName not found."
            throw $ErrorMessage
        } else{
            Write-Error -Message $_.Exception.Message
            throw $_.Exception
        }
    }

    Select-AzureRmSubscription -SubscriptionId $SubscriptionID
    $RG = Get-AzureRmResourceGroup -Name $ResourceGroup
    Foreach($VMName in $VMNames){
        $AzureVM = Get-AzureRmVM -Name $VMName -ResourceGroupName $RG.ResourceGroupName
    
        $Params = @{
            ResourceGroupName = $ResourceGroup
            VMName = $AzureVM.Name
            StorageAccountName = $StorageAccount
            StorageAccountKey = $StorageAccountKey
            StorageContainer = $StorageContainer
            FileName = $ScriptName
            ExtensionName = $ExtensionName
            UploadScript = $UploadScript
        }

        Invoke-AzureRmVmScript @Params -ScriptBlock $ScriptBlock -Force -Verbose
    }
}
Catch{
    Write-Error -Message $_.Exception.Message
    Exit Throw $_
}

content:
TL;DR I wanted to draw graphs in powershell without any external dependancies. So I did, results below.

How to graph:
Create one or more array of points
Join arrays into another array of lines
Execute Draw-Graph function with some data

#Build graph
[Array]$Line1 = 1..12 | ForEach-Object{Get-Random (10..20)}
$p=Get-Random (14..25)
$p%5
[Array]$Line2 = 1..12 | ForEach-Object{
    If($p%5 -eq 0){
        $p-=(get-random (1..3))
    }
    Else{
        $p+=(get-random (1..5))
    }
    $p
}
[Array]$Lines = $Line1,$Line2
$Legend = "Line1 Header","Line2 Header"
$Colors = "Blue","Green"

$file = ([guid]::NewGuid()).Guid
$file = "$env:TEMP\$file.png"
Draw-Graph -Lines $Lines -Legend $Legend -Colors $Colors -Header "Header" -SaveDestination $file
.$file

Graph functions/Initialization

Add-Type -AssemblyName System.Windows.Forms,System.Drawing

Function Get-Color{
    $rbg = @()

    For($i = 0;$i -le 3;$i++){
        Switch($i){
            #Black
            0{ $rbg += 255}#Get-Random -Minimum 128 -Maximum 255 }
            #RGB
            Default{$rbg += Get-Random -Minimum 0 -Maximum 255}
        }
    }
    Return $rbg
}

Function Draw-Graph{
Param(
    $Width = 1024,
    $Height = 512,
    [Array]$Lines,
    [Array]$Legend,
    [Array]$Colors,
    $Header = "Graph",
    $SaveDestination,
    [Switch]$Preview
)
    Begin{}
    Process{
    If($Preview){
        [Windows.Forms.Form]$Window = New-Object System.Windows.Forms.Form
    
        $Window.Width = $Width
        $Window.Height = $Height

        $Window.Show()
        $Window.Refresh()

        [Drawing.Graphics]$Graph = $Window.CreateGraphics()
    }
    Else{
        $bmp = New-Object Drawing.Bitmap $Width,$Height
        $Graph = [Drawing.Graphics]::FromImage($bmp)
            
    }
    $Graph.InterpolationMode = [Drawing.Drawing2D.InterpolationMode]::HighQualityBicubic
    $Graph.SmoothingMode = [Drawing.Drawing2D.SmoothingMode]::AntiAlias
    $Graph.TextRenderingHint = [Drawing.Text.TextRenderingHint]::AntiAlias
    $Graph.CompositingQuality = [Drawing.Drawing2D.CompositingQuality]::HighQuality

    $Background = [System.Drawing.Color]::Snow
    $Graph.Clear($Background)

    $TextBrush = New-Object Drawing.SolidBrush([System.Drawing.Color]::FromArgb(255, 0, 212,252))
    $Font = New-object System.Drawing.Font("arial",12)  
    $gridPen = [Drawing.Pens]::LightGray
        
    #Draw Graph area
    $DrawArea = New-Object 'object[,]' 2,2
    
    # X (Width)
    [int]$DrawArea[0,0] = $Width/10
    [int]$DrawArea[0,1] = ($Width-$Width/6)
    # Y (Height)
    [int]$DrawArea[1,0] = $Height/10
    [int]$DrawArea[1,1] = ($Height-$Height/3)

    # Get X bounds
    $xFac = ($Lines | ForEach-Object{$_.Length} | Sort -Descending)[0]-1
    $xInc = ($DrawArea[0,1]-$DrawArea[0,0]+$DrawArea[0,0])/$xFac 

    #Get Y bounds
    $yMax = ($lines | ForEach-Object{$_} | sort -Descending)[0]
    $yFac = ($DrawArea[1,1]-$DrawArea[1,0])/$yMax

    #Draw box
    $Graph.DrawRectangle($gridPen, ($DrawArea[0,0]),($DrawArea[1,0]),($DrawArea[0,1]),($DrawArea[1,1]))

    #Draw Header
    $Textpoint = New-Object System.Drawing.PointF ((($DrawArea[0,1]-$DrawArea[0,0])/2+$DrawArea[0,0]),($DrawArea[1,0]/2))
    $Graph.DrawString($Header,$Font,$TextBrush,$TextPoint)

    #Draw horizontal lines
    $scaleFac = 0.1
    $i = 1
    #Get scale
    While($i -ge 1){
        $scaleFac = $scaleFac*10
        $i = $yMax/$scaleFac
    }
    $scaleFac = $scaleFac/10

    0..($yMax/$scaleFac) | ForEach-Object{
        $y = $DrawArea[1,1]-(($_*$scaleFac)*$yFac)+$DrawArea[1,0]
        $x1 = $DrawArea[0,0]
        $x2 = $DrawArea[0,1]+$DrawArea[0,0]

        $Graph.DrawLine($gridPen,$x1,$y,$x2,$y)
        $thisPoint = New-Object System.Drawing.PointF (($x1-10),($y-15))
        $thisSF = New-object System.Drawing.StringFormat
        $thisSF.Alignment = "Far"
        $Graph.DrawString("$($_*$scaleFac)",$Font,$TextBrush,$thisPoint,$thisSF)
    }

    If($lines[0].Count -le 1){
        $tmp = $Lines
        Remove-Variable Lines
        $Lines = @(0)
        $Lines[0] = $tmp
        Remove-Variable tmp
        $Lines
    }

    #DRAW LINE
    $l = 0
    Foreach($Line in $Lines){
        If($Colors.Count -gt $l){
            $Pen = New-Object Drawing.Pen($Colors[$l])
        }
        Else{
            $rgb = Get-Color
            $Pen = New-object Drawing.Pen([System.Drawing.Color]::FromArgb($rgb[0],$rgb[1],$rgb[2],$rgb[3]))
        }
        $Pen.Width = 2

        #Initiate/Reset Points
        $Points = @()
        $Step = 0

        Foreach($point in $line){
            
            $x = ($xInc*$step)+$DrawArea[0,0]
            $y = $DrawArea[1,1]-($point*$yFac)+$DrawArea[1,0]

            $Points += New-Object System.Drawing.PointF($x,$y)
            $Step++
        }
        $Graph.DrawLines($pen,$Points)

        If($Legend.Count -gt $l){
            $thisLegend = $Legend[$l]
            If($Colors.Count -gt $l){
                $thisBrush = New-Object Drawing.SolidBrush($Colors[$l])
            }
            Else{
                $rgb = Get-Color
                $thisBrush = New-Object Drawing.SolidBrush([System.Drawing.Color]::FromArgb($rgb[0],$rgb[1],$rgb[2],$rgb[3]))
            }
                 
            $y = $DrawArea[1,1]+$DrawArea[1,0]+20
            $x = $DrawArea[0,0]+100*$l
                
            $thisPoint = New-Object System.Drawing.PointF ($x,$y)
            $thisFont = New-Object System.Drawing.Font("arial",12,[System.Drawing.FontStyle]::Bold)
            $Graph.DrawString($thisLegend,$thisFont,$thisBrush,$thisPoint)
        }
        $l++
    }
     
    }
    End{
        
        If($Preview){
            Start-Sleep 10
        }
        Else{
            $bmp.save($SaveDestination)
        }

        Try{$Graph.Dispose()}Catch{}
        Try{$bmp.Dispose()}Catch{}
        Try{$Window.Close()}Catch{}
        Try{$Window.Dispose()}Catch{}
    }
}

content:
To compliment my earlier post I have created a short function to generate keys.

Function Generate-key{
Param(
    [validateset(128,192,256)]
    $bits,
    [switch]$COUT,
    $seed
)
    $bytes = $bits/8
    $array = @()
    If($seed){
        1..$bytes | ForEach-Object{
            $array += Get-Random -Minimum 0 -Maximum 255 -SetSeed $seed
        }
    }
    Else{
        1..$bytes | ForEach-Object{
            $array += Get-Random -Minimum 0 -Maximum 255
        }
    }

        Return $retval
    }
    Else{

    }
}

title: Encrypting strings with custom keys in powershell
excerpt: Since the ConvertTo-SecureString is not really secure, and neither is the EncodedCommand (base64string) I made two short functions to encrypt and decrypt strings in order to send them across the void unharmed. Function Encrypt-String{ Param( [Parameter( Mandatory=$True, Position=0, ValueFromPipeLine=$true )] [Alias(“String”)] [String]$PlainTextString, [Parameter( Mandatory=$True, Position=1 )] [Alias(“Key”)] [byte[]]$EncryptionKey ) Try{ $secureString = Convertto-SecureString $PlainTextString -AsPlainText […]
content:
Since the ConvertTo-SecureString is not really secure, and neither is the EncodedCommand (base64string) I made two short functions to encrypt and decrypt strings in order to send them across the void unharmed.

Function Encrypt-String{
Param(
    
    [Parameter(
        Mandatory=$True,
        Position=0,
        ValueFromPipeLine=$true
    )]
    [Alias("String")]
    [String]$PlainTextString,
    
    [Parameter(
        Mandatory=$True,
        Position=1
    )]
    [Alias("Key")]
    [byte[]]$EncryptionKey
)
    Try{
        $secureString = Convertto-SecureString $PlainTextString -AsPlainText -Force
        $EncryptedString = ConvertFrom-SecureString -SecureString $secureString -Key $EncryptionKey

        return $EncryptedString
    }
    Catch{Throw $_}

}

this function accepts a string, a key and outputs the encryptedstring.

To encrypt call the function with a plaintext string and a key. the key must be a byte array with 16,24 or 32 bytes (128,192 or 256 bits)

Calling the function looks like this.

$string = @'
I am about to become encrypted!
'@

[Byte[]]$Key = 117,9,103,192,133,20,53,149,81,95,108,34,81,224,226,220,56,68,133,120,139,241,176,239,171,54,231,205,83,57,51,255

$EncryptedString = Encrypt-String -PlainTextString $string -Key $Key

The output becomes 

PS> $encryptedString
76492d1116743f0423413b16050a5345MgB8AG8AVABnAGcAagArAFYAUgBoAGkAYwBOAFIAZgBTAGEAQQB1AGsAMQBmAHcAPQA9
AHwAZQBiADIAOAA4ADQAYwA5ADEAMABlAGMAOABmADUAOAAyAGIANQAzADIAOABjADIAOAAxADUAZgAxADYAMgAyAGQAMgA2AGUA
ZQA2ADYANAA2AGUAYQA0AGMAMgBmADMAYgAwADIAMgAxAGQAOQAxADcANwBhADgANwAxADcAZgBjADEANwAxADcANwA1ADgANwBh
ADMAMgA3AGEAMABmADcAYQAzADcAYQBiADgANAAwADkAOQA4ADgANgA1AGYAMwA5ADMANAA3ADkAZgAwAGIAZAA1AGQAZgA2AGEA
MABmADIANwBmADkANQBhAGYAOAAxAGYANgA0ADAAOAAxAA==

Now to the decrypt. This function needs the exact encryptedstring and the exact key that the string was encoded with.

Function Decrypt-String{
Param(
    [Parameter(
        Mandatory=$True,
        Position=0,
        ValueFromPipeLine=$true
    )]
    [Alias("String")]
    [String]$EncryptedString,

    [Parameter(
        Mandatory=$True,
        Position=1
    )]
    [Alias("Key")]
    [byte[]]$EncryptionKey
)
    Try{
        $SecureString = ConvertTo-SecureString $EncryptedString -Key $EncryptionKey
        $bstr = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::SecureStringToBSTR($SecureString)
        [string]$String = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::PtrToStringAuto($bstr)
        [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::ZeroFreeBSTR($bstr)

        Return $String
    }
    Catch{Throw $_}

}

To call this function simply input the encryptedString and key and you get the pre-encrypted string as the return value.

PS> Decrypt-String -EncryptedString $EncryptedString -EncryptionKey $Key
I am about to become encrypted!

Both functions accept value by pipeline so a Get-content can be used like this.

Get-Content C:\temp\encrypted.txt | Decrypt-String -EncryptionKey $Key

An overkill version of this is to double encode/encrypt. First convert the string to a base64 (encodedCommand style) then encode it with the key. This really adds no further security except to obfuscate the encrypted package and in case someone gets the key to decrypt they have to convert the encodedcommand to a string from base 64

Function Encrypt-String{
Param(
    
    [Parameter(
        Mandatory=$True,
        Position=0,
        ValueFromPipeLine=$true
    )]
    [Alias("String")]
    [String]$PlainTextString,
    
    [Parameter(
        Mandatory=$True,
        Position=1
    )]
    [Alias("Key")]
    [byte[]]$EncryptionKey
)
    Try{
        $bytes = [System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode.GetBytes($PlainTextString)
        $encodedCommand = [Convert]::ToBase64String($bytes)
        $secureString = Convertto-SecureString $encodedCommand -AsPlainText -Force
        $EncryptedString = ConvertFrom-SecureString -SecureString $secureString -Key $EncryptionKey

        return $EncryptedString
    }
    Catch{Throw $_}

}


Function Decrypt-String{
Param(
    [Parameter(
        Mandatory=$True,
        Position=0,
        ValueFromPipeLine=$true
    )]
    [Alias("String")]
    [String]$EncryptedString,

    [Parameter(
        Mandatory=$True,
        Position=1
    )]
    [Alias("Key")]
    [byte[]]$EncryptionKey
)
    Try{
        $SecureString = ConvertTo-SecureString $EncryptedString -Key $EncryptionKey
        $bstr = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::SecureStringToBSTR($SecureString)
        [string]$String = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::PtrToStringAuto($bstr)
        [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::ZeroFreeBSTR($bstr)

        $data = @()
        [convert]::FromBase64String($encodedCommand) | ForEach-Object{
            If($_ -ne 0){
                $data += [char]$_
            }
        }

        Return ($data -join '')
    }
    Catch{Throw $_}

}

Function To-Roman{
Param([Parameter(Mandatory=$true)][int]$int)
    [int]$M = 1000
    [int]$D = 500
    [int]$C = 100
    [int]$L = 50
    [int]$X = 10
    [int]$V = 5
    [int]$I = 1
    If($int -eq 0){Throw "Zero does not exist in roman culture.";Return 404}
    $done = $false
    While($done -eq $false){

        #$Roman = $roman+(addup $int $m "M")
        If($int -ge $m){
            $n = Loopy $int $m
            $int = $n[0]

        }

        If($int -ge $D){
            $n = Loopy $int $D
            $int = $n[0]

        }

        If($int -ge $C){

        If($int -ge $L){

        If($int -ge $X){

        }

        If($int -ge $V){
            $n = Loopy $int $V
            $int = $n[0]
            1..$n[1] | %{$Roman = $Roman+"V"}
        }

        If($int -ge $I){
            $n = Loopy $int $I
            $int = $n[0]
            1..$n[1] | %{$Roman = $Roman+"I"}
            
        }
        If($roman.Contains("CCCC")){$roman=$Roman.Replace("CCCC","CD")}
        If($roman.Contains("XXXX")){$roman=$Roman.Replace("XXXX","XC")}
        If($roman.Contains("LLLL")){$roman=$Roman.Replace("LLLL","XL")}
        If($roman.Contains("LXXX")){$roman=$Roman.Replace("LXXX","XC")}
        If($roman.Contains("VIV")){$roman=$Roman.Replace("VIV","IX")}
        If($roman.Contains("IIII")){$roman=$Roman.Replace("IIII","IV")}

        If($int -eq 0){$done = $true}
    }
    Return $Roman
}

Function Loopy{
Param(
    [int]$int,
    [int]$number
)
    $notDone = $true
    $loops = 0
    While($notDone){
        If($int-$number -ge 0){$int=$int-$number;$loops++}
        ElseIf($int-$number -lt $number){$notDone = $false}
    }
    return $int,$loops
}

content:
Function Invoke-GUI {
<#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Invoke-GUI creates a customizable threaded GUI for powershell
    .DESCRIPTION
        Creates a GUI from XAML file through Windows Presentation Foundation.
        All XAML data that require changeable data requires a "Name" node which sets the variable name
        Any XML nodes with name will get a variable assigned under $Code. and all subsequent data is accessible from there.
        The main GUI will be assigned $Code.GUI
    .PARAMETER File
        Sets a file with the XAML data used to build the interface.
    .PARAMETER XAML
        Input object in form on an already created XML variable.
    .PARAMETER OnTick
        Code to be executed on each tick
    .PARAMETER InitializationScript
        Code to be performed one time before the GUI shows.
    .PARAMETER TimerInterval
        Timer interval
    .PARAMETER LogFile
        LogFile location
    .Example
        Invoke-GUI -File C:\Application\GUI.xaml
        This loads the GUI without any tick action or custom initialization script.
    .Example
        Invoke-GUI -XAML $XAML -LogFile C:\Application\dump.log
        Loads the GUI from an already compiled XAML object and outputs logs to dump.log
    .Example
        Invoke-GUI -XAML $XAML -OnTick {$Code.MessageBox.Content = "Random number: $(Get-Random)"} -TimerInterval "0:1:0.00" -LogFile C:\Application\dump.log
        As example two but updates a MessageBox variable with a random number once per minute.
    .Example
        Invoke-GUI -XAML $XAML -TimerInterval "0:1:0.00" -LogFile C:\Application\dump.log -OnTick {
            $Code.MessageBox.Content = "Random number: $(Get-Random)"
        } -InitializationScript {
            $Code.Company.Content = "Contoso"
            $Code.Agreement.Value = 0
        }
        As example three but adds some company and agreement information at startup.
#>
[cmdletbinding()]
Param (
    [Parameter(Mandatory=$True,ParameterSetName="File")]
    [String]$File,
    [Parameter(Mandatory=$True,ParameterSetName="XAML")]
    [XML]$XAML,
    [Parameter(Mandatory=$False)]
    [ScriptBlock]$OnTick = {},
    [Parameter(Mandatory=$False)]
    [ScriptBlock]$InitializationScript = {},
    [Parameter(Mandatory=$False)]
    [TimeSpan]$TimerInterval = "0:0:1.00",
    [Parameter(Mandatory=$False)]
    [String]$LogFile
)
    
    If($LogFile){
        $time = get-date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
        "$Time | Starting GUI script" | Out-File $LogFile -Append
    }
    
    $Script:Code = [hashtable]::Synchronized(@{})
    $Code.TimerInterval = $TimerInterval
    $Code.OnTick = $OnTick
    $Code.InitializationScript = $InitializationScript
    $Code.ParameterSet = $PSCmdlet.ParameterSetName
    If($PSCmdlet.ParameterSetName -eq "File"){
        $Code.XAMLFile = $File
    }
    Else{
        $Code.XAML = $XAML
    }

    If($LogFile){
        $Code.LogFile = $LogFile
    }

    $Script:Runspacehash = [hashtable]::Synchronized(@{})
    $Runspacehash.host = $Host
    $Runspacehash.runspace = [RunspaceFactory]::CreateRunspace()
    $Runspacehash.runspace.ApartmentState = “STA”
    $Runspacehash.runspace.ThreadOptions = “ReuseThread”
    $Runspacehash.runspace.Open() 
    $Runspacehash.psCmd = {Add-Type -AssemblyName PresentationCore,PresentationFramework,WindowsBase}.GetPowerShell()
    $Runspacehash.runspace.SessionStateProxy.SetVariable("code",$Code)
    $Runspacehash.runspace.SessionStateProxy.SetVariable("Runspacehash",$Runspacehash)
    $Runspacehash.psCmd.Runspace = $Runspacehash.runspace
    

    $Runspacehash.Handle = $Runspacehash.psCmd.AddScript({ 

        $Script:Update = {
            # Do stuff on tick here
            .$Code.OnTick
        }

        If($Code.ParameterSet -eq "File"){[XML]$XAML = Get-Content $Code.XAMLFile}
        Else{[XML]$XAML = $Code.XAML}

        # builds gui as $Code.GUI with data from $XAML
        # creates variable for each xml property with the "name" assigned.
        Try {

            [reflection.assembly]::loadwithpartialname("System.Windows.Forms") | Out-Null

            $objXMLReader = (New-Object System.Xml.XmlNodeReader $XAML)
            $Code.GUI = [Windows.Markup.XamlReader]::Load($objXMLReader)
        
            $Code.GUI.WindowStartupLocation = "CenterScreen"

            If($Code.LogFile){
                $time = get-date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
                "$Time | Creating variables for XAML elements.." | Out-File $Code.LogFile -Append
            }
            $XAML.SelectNodes("//*[@Name]") | ForEach-Object {
                If($Code.LogFile){
                    $time = get-date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
                    "$Time | Variable created: `$Code.$($_.Name)" | Out-File $Code.LogFile -Append
                }
                $Code."$($_.Name)" = $Code.GUI.FindName($_.Name)
            }
        }
        Catch {
            If($Code.LogFile){
                $time = get-date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
                "$Time | $_" | Out-File $Code.LogFile -Append
            }
            Exit        
        }

        #Timer Event
        $Code.GUI.Add_SourceInitialized({
            $Script:timer = new-object System.Windows.Threading.DispatcherTimer 
            If($Code.LogFile){
                $time = get-date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
                "$Time | Timer interval is: $($Code.TimerInterval)" | Out-File $Code.LogFile -Append
            }
            $timer.Interval = [TimeSpan]$Code.TimerInterval
        
            $timer.Add_Tick({
                $Update.Invoke()
                [Windows.Input.InputEventHandler]{$Code.GUI.UpdateLayout()}
            })
        
            #Start timer
            If($Code.LogFile){
                $time = get-date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
                "$Time | Starting timer" | Out-File $Code.LogFile -Append
            }
            $timer.Start()
            If (-NOT $timer.IsEnabled) {

                If($Code.LogFile){
                    $time = get-date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
                    "$Time | Stopping GUI" | Out-File $Code.LogFile -Append
                }

                $Code.GUI.Close()
            }
        }) 

        $Code.GUI.Add_Closed({
            If($Code.LogFile){
                $time = get-date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
                "$Time | GUI disposed" | Out-File $Code.LogFile -Append
            }
            $timer.Stop()
            $Runspacehash.PowerShell.Dispose()
    
            [gc]::Collect()
            [gc]::WaitForPendingFinalizers()    
        })

        Try{$Code.InitializationScript.Invoke()}
        Catch{
            If($Code.LogFile){
                $time = get-date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
                "$Time | $_" | Out-File $Code.LogFile -Append
            }
        }

        # Does not work to place this in the InitializationScript yet. Need to work around this somehow
        $Code.GUI.Add_MouseLeftButtonDown({
            $This.DragMove()
        })

        
        $Code.GUI.ShowDialog() | Out-Null

    }).BeginInvoke()

    #Give gui time to initialize
    Start-sleep 1
}

Function Update-GUI{
<#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Update-GUI Sends a scriptblock for execution in the GUI thread.
    .DESCRIPTION
        Takes a Scriptblock for execution in the GUI thread.
        It is a simple command (9 rows) but as it is used often converted to a function.
        Code is:
        $Code.GUI.Dispatcher.Invoke([action]{
            Try{.$ScriptBlock}
            Catch{
                If($Code.LogFile){
                    $time = get-date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
                    "$Time | Could not execute command: $ScriptBlock" | Out-File $Code.LogFile -Append
                }
            }    
        })
    .PARAMETER ScriptBlock
        Scriptblock to run inside thread.
    .Example
        Update-GUI -ScriptBlock {$Code.Message.content = "Hello world"}
        Updates the message node content with "hello world"
#>
Param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory=$True)]
    [ScriptBlock]$ScriptBlock
) 
    $Code.GUI.Dispatcher.Invoke([action]{
        Try{.$ScriptBlock}
        Catch{
            If($Code.LogFile){
                $time = get-date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss"
                "$Time | Could not execute command: $ScriptBlock" | Out-File $Code.LogFile -Append
            }
        }    
    })
}

content:
A while back I made a quick hotfix indexer script and database browser.

These were not too great but had sufficient functionality for the time. Now that I have expanded on functionality I want to write this as a single post.

Any Microsoft enterprise technician could see the value in having a list like this.
The question is why Microsoft don’t provide this list themselves.
Anyhow, let’s begin!

This package contains three files. One indexer.ps1. One HotfixBrowser.ps1 and a config file where you specify SQL connectionstring and table to be used before running the scripts.

The heart of the script is the indexer. It goes through a range specified and lists them in a database. The table must have the following columns:

Other columns can be added if needed and will be listed in the hotfix browser.
What I do is add a scheduled task that runs this script with a set of ranges every weekend to get a up-to date view.

When the indexer has completed you can start HotfixBrowser.ps1

From here you can search with standard SQL syntax. All fields to a LIKE search so for example All windows 8 hotfixes released during 2014 has this search criteria.

Clicking search allows you to quickly see the short text of all articles involving Windows 8 with a hotfix download available allowing you to work efficiently and determine if any of the hotfixes are applicable to your client environment.

There are also the option to go ‘advanced’ which allows you to edit the Select query as you see fit.

In the File menu you can export the current datatable as a CSV file.
In the tools mode you can save and load searches as well as choose visible columns and enable edit mode.
Edit mode makes the cells writable and allows you to send a UPDATE query to the server (given the appropriate rights) to edit some fields such as note and other custom fields.

Looking around and asking on communities this seems often to be due to when the stepper motors […]
content:
With all the mechanical parts assembled all that is left is firmware calibration – or so we thought.

With all basic calibration done we noticed on prints that the X and Y axises were shifting. as shown below. Looking around and asking on communities this seems often to be due to when the stepper motors skips steps or the timing belt slipping.
We tried everything suggested, from cooling stepper drivers, motors, tightening belts and turning down acceleration in the firmware but nothing worked.

It was first when we loosened the belts and ran the motors we noticed that the pulleys were slipping off the shafts. This was because the pulleys screws were biting into the brass pipe which we used to bridge the gap between our motors and the pulleys did not provide enough friction. When we loosened the belts even less friction was applied between the brass and drive shaft and the slippage became apparent.        

After buying some metal epoxy to fixate everything together we are able to finally produce perfectly straight prints!


The print above are some holders for a spool where I designed the feet myself.
It’s quite an amazing feeling to draw something in a 3D program one day and to hold it the next.

With all the parts delivered it was time to assemble.

I’m not going to go through the whole build process. But it consisted of loads of screwing around (pun intended) and It’s not the prettiest build but i honestly don’t care about looks. It’s function I’m after.

To make a long story short here are some pictures of the build process:

     


    

One issue we had was that the motors shaft diameter was 4mm and the pulleys had 5mm. We solved this by buying a brass pipe with 4mm inner and 5mm outer diameter.
We then cut the pipe and screwed them on. This kept the pulleys from rotating in an elipse and gave us a nice smooth circular and even rotation.

Not being the most experianced DIY guys we spent about half a billion hours on assembly. But in the end it worked and we managed to produce our first ever print!

Success!!!

    Function Process-SQLCmd {
    Param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory=$true)]
        [String]$Command,
        [Parameter(Mandatory=$false)]
        [String]$ConnectionString = 'Server=LocalHost\SQL;Database=ClientMaintenance;Trusted_Connection=True;'
    )
